div.head: POULTRY FOR PROFIT.
div.p: POULTRY FOR PROFIT.
THIS WEEK'S WORK IN BRIEF.

The chickens will now be able to find a large quantity of natural food. They should be encouraged to range freely. When ground is to be turned over preparatory to sowing both chicks and land will benefit if the heaps are placed within easy reach. Get the chicks on to sound oats and wheat as soon as possible. Examine the heads of chicks occasionally for lice. And if affected apply the cure at once. Where it takes the form of oil us every spar- ingly. Eggs for sitting are now in great demand. And an advertisement will quickly repay its cost. . .
Protect the chicks from the strong winds. Sheep hurdles covered with sacking will serve the purpose. Watle hurdles are also cheap and useful.

In the fine and warm weather the chicks are apt to stray, and the numbers should be checke I every evening. Keep the grass short round the house sides. It is a frequent cause of wood rot. More eggs will be required during Easter week, and the prices are improving. The laying stock should therefore be kept "'up to concert pitch." A little more stimulat• ing diet will effect this.—" Poultry World.:"

div.head: GOOD STORY.
div.p: A GOOD STORY.

Here is a good yarn from the "Staffordshire Sentinel." An innocent-looking lady came up to the door and pleaded the cause of an "invalid friend," asking "Have you a shillingsworth of eggs to spare, please?" "Yes, certainly, coma inside." The lady, by way of introduction, re- marked that she had heard that this friend of mine had always plenty of "big brown eggs" and "right through the bad weather." Yes that was the case. My friend proceeded to bring the egg basket out, calling forth an ex- clamation of pleased surprise from the would- be purchaser. Then he brought out the "doc- toring needle," and started to prick the -hells of the " shillingsworth "in full view. "Oh! what are you doing that for?" The reply came that the eggs would not be damaged for eating purposes. "But," said the visitor, "they will be no use to me now." " Oh!" said the poultry- keeper, "my sittings are seven and, sixpence— Good afternoon!" Exit the nonplussed egg-pur- chasing-for-invalid-friend philanthropist.

div.head: EARLY CHICKS.
div.p: THE EARLY CHICKS.

Some of the December and early January hatched birds are now ready for killing, says "Feathered World," but any backward ones should be given some soft food and kept together in small runs. To anyone using the cramming- machine this will not apply, because then the birds are bound to have what food is prepared. But a very nice chicken can be had by feeding soft food on a grass run by just giving all they will eat, and then clearing the rest away. Birds so treated should be kept quiet and not given water, but the food made rather more moist than usual. The giving of water prevents the increase of weight, and has the tendency to harden the flesh. As soon as these birds are ready for table and you can find a market, let them go, because this will reduce expense and mean a larger percentage of profit. The pullets will be best kept on for egg-produc- tion, for all these are sadly neeaed. if only to help along our wounded soldiers. What a pity that so many of the eggs sent to the hospitals are unusable, and, in fact, some are putrid Better not give at all than give rubbish.

div.head: BITS FOR BEGINNERS.
div.p: BITS FOR BEGINNERS.
The Corn Bin.

All corn bins should be made rat-proof; this may be done by nailing tin on the inside round all the joints. See that the corn bin is not too large or the grain may become heated, and there- fore dangerous to use. Meals should also be stored in small quantities, or it will become musty, and when fed in this condition is the cause of much trouble.

•The Addled and Other Useless Eggs. At the, end of 'every test or hatch the addled and dead-in-shell eggs should be buried. Do not leave them in the incubator, the foul gases they 3enerate are harmful to the incubating eggs. Neither should they be left about outside, since they will attract vermin. Bury them deeply, and cover them in such a way that it will 13 impossible for dogs, cats, or rats to scratch them up.

Save the Feathers. Where a few birds are to be killed it will be worth while to save the feathers. Should the quantity be worth marketing, the prices realised will be very high. When the quantity does not justify the trouble of taking or sending to
market, they can be made into a fine pillow or cushion.
Starting Now.

A cheap start may yet be made by means f day-old chickens or by purchasing growing chickens. Eggs from light breeds, may yet bo set, but the heavy breeds, if set, for hatchin; now, would not prove very satisfactory a 3 winter layers. Clearing the Pens. _ _

Where the breeding pens are to be broken up and the pens cleared it will be best to allow the pens to remain vacant for a few weeks; this will make the ground much fresher for the chickens. The litter in the scratching sheds should b? changed, and any repairs needed should be done at once.—" The Poultry World."
"The Feathered World."

div.head: FEEDING MENUS. April.
div.p: FEEDING MENUS. April.

Sunday.—Breakfast, 7 to 8 a.m. : Soft food, composed of one part each biscuit 'meal, pea meal, bran, and fish meal, and six parts thirds, mixed to a moist, crumbly consistency. Dinner, 12 to 1 p.m.: A handful or two of dari and buck- wheat or other grain, and this should be scat- tered amongst the litter in the scratching shed. Last feed of day, 5 to 6 p.m.: Grain, consisting of wheat screenings, oats, and split maize in equal parts. Monday.—Breakfast: Grain, oats. At noon give a little fresh-cut green bone or boiled and minced lights, allowing, if the birds are in full lay, an ounce or more to each fowl, and this will tend to keep up the egg supply. Last feed: Soft food, composed of the previous day's scraps, boiled and mixed to a crumbly consistency with bran and maize meal, one part each, and thirds three parts. Tuesday.—Breakfast: Soft food, composed of four parts thirds, two parts each pea meal and bran, and one part meat or fish meal. If malt culms can be procured, these can be used in place of pea meal, and the best results would be obtained by well scalding or boiling them before adding same to the mash. At noon a handful or two of small grain should be scat- tered amongst the litter in the scratching shed. Last feed: Grain, wheat or wheat screenings. Wednesday.—Breakfast: train, a mixture of wheat and oats. At noon give a little green bone. minced lights, or meat scraps from the tablo. Last feed: Soft food, composed of four parts thirds, two parts each barley meal and bran, and one part fish or meat meal.
Thursday.—As on Sunday. Friday.—As on Monday.

Saturday.—As on Tuesday. Once a week a small piece of sulphate of iron, the size of a pea or small bean, should be di- solved in water and added to the soft food. This will act as a tonic and tend to keep thp birds in a good healthy condition. Where birds are kept on earth runs, fresh green food should be supplied every day, this being essential to their well-being. Twice a week sharp.flint grit and oyster shell should be given, and this shouli be placed in a small box in the corner of the scratching shed or somewhere under cover.

div.head: CHICKENS ON A FREE RANGE.
div.p: CHICKENS ON A FREE RANGE.

A flock of chickens will not roam continu- ously over any range for a complete day. A little observation will indicate the number qf hours each flock takes full advantage of the open run; and when this period has elapsed the birds should be returnod to their deep litter and cage enclosure, and the range should be devoted to another brood. Under such a system of manage- ment a given area of grass land will carry a much larger number of chickens, says the "Poultry World."

div.head: CHANCE OF A LIFETIME.
div.p: THE CHANCE OF A LIFETIME.

Some light on the egg problem is shown by the Board of Trade figures. In the week ending April Bth, we imported only 37,242 great hundreds; in the corresponding week of 1914 the numh-r was 326,713. In the same week our poultry im- ports were of the value of £1,533 only; in 1911 the value was 09,282. Evidently, says "Farm and Home," th- British poultry keeper has the opportunity of his life.

div.head: TAINTED SOIL.
div.p: TAINTED SOIL.

Contrary to general belief, it is not only fowls which are closely confined in runs that are liable to suffer from tainted soil. Unfortun- ately, the trouble is nearly as prevalent on farms where space is practically unlimited. The reason for this is that the fowls are usually all kept together in a position where cropping is not always an easy matter—say, for instance, near the homestead, which is well beaten down and is more of a track than pasture land. There is only one remedy under these conditions, that is to remove the fowls and well lime the land in the proportion of 3 tons to the acre, and allow to remain fallow for eight or nine months.

div.head: BLOOD AND GREEN FOOD.
div.p: BLOOD AND GREEN FOOD.

A very valuable addition to the morning mash is fresh blood, which largely takes the place meat. It should be mixed with the meals in the place of water, forming the whole into a crumbly moist condition. Blood may be kept for a week or ten days if it is boiled, but when living near a slaughter house the best plan is to procure it every second day and supply it in a fresh condition, for in this state it possesses a much better feeding value. The benefits of green food, particularly when fowls are confined in runs, can scarcely be overestimated. Grass, lettuces, cabbage leaves; (tc., are all excellent for the purpose. and, as a rule, are plentiful, with perhaps the exception of the lettuces. Mangels, swedes, and turnips are likewise bene- ficial; a• half root suspended to within a few inches of the ground not only helps to keep the systems of the birds in good working order, but it also affords them exercise and amusement.

div.head: FEEDING YOUNG STOCK.
div.p: FEEDING YOUNG STOCK.

Upon the early feeding of chickens very much of their future value depends. Most poultry- keepers realise this fact, and look after the birds very carefully during the first few weeks during their lives. But very often when the birds have got beyond the chicken age, the early care is left off.-,..50. far as half-grown chickens are concerned, their growth must be maintained, at the same time the food must not , be of a too forcing nature, or some of the more precocious pullets may come on to lay. This must be discouraged in every way possible, since nothing undermines the constitution of pullets to the same extent as commencing to lay before they have reached the natural age for them to do so. When they give signs of laying soft food and everything of a stimulating character should be discontinued. The staple grain, from the time that the youngsters are big enough to take it, should be plump oats. This will foster growth, repair the• bodily waste, and lay up a reserve of stamina which will stand the birds in good stead when the time arrives for them to enter the breeding pens, or to be numbered ,:imong the laying flock.—" Farm and Home."

div.head: kmuiT (3,116WiX6 6N CANADIAN
div.p: kmuiT (3,116WiX6 6N CANADIAN
PRAIRIES.

Fruit growing is slowly making progress on parts of the Canadian Prairies. It hA been suggested in the Dominion Parliament that the Experimental Farm at Lethbridge, Alberta, should $y particular attention to this question. There is .already on the farm ,an orchard of several hundred trees where apples as Well as small fruits are being raised, and it was pro- 'posed that an expert should be located at the statl9n. In many parts of the irrigated dis- trict there have..bepn quite remarkable crops of first-class apples. It was also suggested that farmers be permitted to visit the experimental farm at Lethbridge and remain for a week or so for studying and investigation. A fruit station is being established at Morden, Manitoba, where particular attention will be given to the study of• fruit raising in Western Canada.

div.head: Maister's Presence.
div.p: The Maister's Presence.

Some thirty years ago I met, a• farmer, a wise, active, diligent man , who always worked with his nien in the fields both in spring and in har- vest. In the worst days, the hard 'eighties, when many farmers succumbed because of losses, he seemed to thrive, and I asked him how it was be was so successful. He said, "It's very simple. I taak' it a rule ,to rise' wi' the me, and to see them yoke .ilka mornin.' Ye. see the maister's presence is the farmer's prat. I 'hae aye , foun' that my am n en is the best grieve.. When. a fairmer lives in his work hell get a livin" by his wark.'---" The North-TAgt, Parmer and Cottar."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 22, 1916.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 22, 1916.
FARM AND GARDEN.
ROYAL SHOW AND RAILWAY TRAFFIC.

It is reported that an agitation is taking place in trading circles in Manchester for the prohi- bition of the Royal Agricultural Show. The ground is that it will increase the congestion of railway traffic. It will be remembered that negotiations between the Ministry of Munitions on the subject were referred to at a recent meet- ing of the Council, but it is believed that a satisfactory arrangement has been come to and that the show will take place in due course. The matter was mentioned in the House of Commons on Tuesday, and Mr. Tennant, who replied, said the railway companies did not anticipate any trouble in dealing with railway traffic at the time of the Royal Agricultural Show in Manchester.

div.head: WEATHER AND THE CROPS.
div.p: THE WEATHER AND THE CROPS.

The Crop Reporters of the Board of Agricul- ture in reporting on agricultural conditions in England and Wales, under date April 1, state that the very wet and stormy weather, which was accompanied- by much snow, has caused great delay in all agricultural operations. The early-sown winter wheat has generally with- stood the bad conditions well, and is satisfac- tory, though it has made no progress during the month, and is mostly backward.' Wheat on heavy land, or on land subject to flooding, has, however, suffered a good deal, while that sown late in the autumn is also not satisfactory. The area under wheat appears to be about 7 or 8 per cent. less than last year. Winter oats and beans are mostly healthy and promising crops, although backward, but there are a good- num- ber of exceptions, especially in the West. Preparation of the land for the spring crops was almost at a standstill during the month, and very little corn indeed was sown, none at all being got in in most counties. Similarly, only in one or two very favoured 'districts have a few early potatoes been planted. Seeds are gener- ally strong and vigorous, promising a good or abundant yield, more particularly on the eastern side of the country; in some parts the wet has done some harm, and reports from the north-west are not so favourable as elsewhere.

div.head: Bad for the Lambs.
div.p: Bad for the Lambs.

There has been a good fall of lambs. The abnormally bad weather has resulted in the ewes being only in poor condition, and in many parts they are not milking well. The lambs were generally strong and healthy at birth, but the conditions have been so adverse, that altogether losses have probably been rather over average. Labour is everywhere very defi-, eient, and with considerable arrears to be made. Up, many farmers will be hard put to it to get the work done this spring.

div.head: WHY DANES ARE COMING.
div.p: WHY DANES ARE COMING.

A correspondent of a contemporary, dealing with the fact that Danes are coming over to work on the land, sneers at the suggestion that these representatives of "ideal agricultural prosperity" should be willing to serve "the effete English farmer" for wages. A lot of irri- tating nonsense has doubtless been written about agriculture in Denmark. It is very ques- tionable whether Danish farming is as good as our own, though Danish methods of dealing with agricultural produce may be better, but if Danes have anything to teach the British farmer the latter need not be too proud to learn. In any case these young men are coming over to work—doubtless on terms which satisfy themselves—and as the farmer is short of labour. the arrangement ought to be mutually satisfac- tory. Probably part of the explanation is that the men are hoping to learn something that will extend their own knowledge and experience, says "Farm and Home." If that be so they are to be commended, and if the lessons are reciprocal so much the better.

div.head: HEALTHY COWS FOR CHEESE.
div.p: HEALTHY COWS FOR CHEESE.

A point in the production of milk for cheese is to use only that obtained from healthy cows, otherwise the milk may not be suitable for cheese, however up-to-date the conditions under which it is obtained. If a cow has garget or felon in the udder the milk contains a lot of pus cells which cause small putrid patches to appear in the cheese during the ripening period. The casein of milk is the constituent which is coagulated by the rennet to form the curd, and the more complete the coagulation the more fat is taken in the curd while it is forming. Dirty milk is sometimes contaminated with organisms known as digestive bacteria. These germs digest or dissolve part of the casein, which then passes off in the whey. This results in a low yield of cheese from the milk employed, as in addition to the casein being digested a certfv:n amount of fat.also is lost. The unfortunate part of contaminated milk is that the germs are so minute in size that they cannot be seen by the naked eye, and a great deal of the cow dung in milk is dissolved in the warm milk before it gets strained. If the germs could be seen in the milk, there is no doubt that more care would be taken with its production at most farms. The harmful effect of undesirable germs in milk for butter-making may generally be overcome by pasteurising the milk or cream, then ripening the latter, but for cheese-making the pasteurisation of the milk is not possible for the ordinary cheesemaker.—C. W. Walker- Tisdale in "Farm and Home."

div.head: RUBBISH PILE.
div.p: THE RUBBISH PILE.

On some farms odds and ends of broken imple- ments, old boxes, boards, barrels, hoops, scrap- iron, bones, waggon wheels, and a thousand and one other articles are permitted to accumulate, the idea being that some day everything will '"come in handy." This is a false and often expensive economy. No rubbish heap should be permitted to accumulate on the farm. It is a sign of carelessness. It gives a place a bad appearance; and even reflects upon the charac- ter of the owner. Take pride in your. farm. Have a place for everything; and see that it is kept there; then you will not lose valuable time hunting for a certain monkey-wrench, or the hammer or axe. Rubbish piles are excel- lent places—for rats, snakes, vermin and germs. A certain farmer had his sheds and stables full of old boards and broken boxes. Soon he began to miss,his chicks. In moving some boards he discovered, some twenty dead chicks. A rat had killed and carried them ' there. This 'farmer- lost 100 chicks and many eggs every year. The old boards were only good for firewood, yet he permitted them to accumulate until his, place was full of rats. On another farm, which was also full of rubbish, the rats became, so numerous as to be a nuisance to the farmers in the vicinity. While you are about it, make' a thorough job of it and clean out the- rubbish in the cellar and attic, too. Old shoes, empty , bottles, discarded clothing, broken furniture, and a raft of other things, accumulate as the months and years pass. Somebody else may be able to use this rubbish—sell it, give it 'away, or burn it, hut don't let it litter the house needlessly. H A " rubbish" shop is all right enoughrin its place, but that place is not'on the , average farm. The only shop to have there is a workshop.—" Farm journal,"

div.head: LOOK TO YOUR MACHINES!
div.p: LOOK TO YOUR MACHINES!

. The . President of the Board of Agriculture and Fisheries .desires to impress upon farmers the necessity of having their agricultural machinery overhauled at the earliest possible date, and of ordering at once the spate or repair parts necessary to put the machines into good working order. Such action will have the effect of relieving considerably the Pyesente .upon the manufacturers Who are working with depleted staffs owing, to enlistment and other causes, and will go far to ensure farmers possessing reliable machines at the time when ~they are. most. needed.- .

div.head: FARMER SLACKERS.
div.p: FARMER SLACKERS.

rarraing is an indispensable business, par- ticularly now, and the depletion of farm tabour is a serious matter, says "Farm and Home." The misguided zeal of th • recruiting sergeant and the irregular methods of recruiting are re- sponsible for a great deal of mischief, and further, the Government as a whole must be blamed. We have .an instance only this week of a married farmer who was the sole worker left on his holding, with a large head of stoek to feed',, being strongly urged to attest. The whole proceeding is ridiculous, in view of the urgent requests made to cultivators and stock owners to keep up the supply of food. On the other hand it is well to rid ourselves of cant and pretence in this matter. 'There are large numbers of slackers on the farm as else.. where, and in far too many cases we fear the object in view has not been to secure the welfare of the crops fso much as to secure remission from a form of national service which •involves both risk to life and a disturbance of settled con-

ditions, farmers must be willing to avail them- selves of what labour is procurable. It is all very well to say a woman is of "no use" on the farm. It may be true enough that a woman, particularly one not trained to farm work, is not as valuable a workei-iis a man.; but a willing female helper can do much useful work and farmers ought to be ready to accept gladly any assistance that is forthcoming. It is a national duty.

div.head: SULPHATE OF AMMONIA.
div.p: SULPHATE OF AMMONIA.

Lord Selborne desires to call the attention of farmers to the fact that the decision to suspend the issue of licences for the export of sulphate of ammonia was based on the assumption that the home demand for this fertiliser would be substantially increased. Unless therefore farmers at once increase their demand, the result will be that stocks will accumulate and the output will be curtailed. In view of the importance of using every effort to stimulate the production of maximum crops during the war, in the interests both of agri- culture and of the nation generally, Lord Sel- borne appeals to farmers to avail themselves without delay of the present opportunity to procure supplies of sulphate of ammonia for spring use. Leaflets dealing with the use of sulphate of ammonia may be obtained free of charge on application to the Secretary, Board of Agri- Culture and '.:Fisheries, 8, Whitehall-place; London, S.W.

div.head: COUNTIES AND ALLIED FARMERS.
div.p: COUNTIES AND ALLIED FARMERS.

The largest individual county contribution to the Agricultural Relief of Allies 'Fund up to the present is that of Cheshire, where three "jumble" sales alone brought in £6,423. The second largest is that of Essex £6,245, raised, singularly enough, without a single jumble sale. Other four-figure counties are: Middlesex £5,302, Kent £4,548, Hunts £3,267, Notts £2,777, Cambridge £2,650, Lanes over £2,000, Sussex £1,977, Northants £1,835, Hants £1,440, Berks £1,352, Derbyshire £1,325, Rutland £1,23/, Yorks £1,205, Oxon £1,071, and Lines £1,009.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

It is an advantage to have in the autumn plenty of bloom in the garden, and such a pic- ture is rarer than many persons suppose. A few years ago we visited a garden in the autumn, and were much struck by the effect of a mass of early flowering chrysanthemums against a background of the Japan anemone. This arrangement proved the value of these two easily managed plants for keeping up a bright display when the days begin to shorten. For cutting the anemone is very useful, and rightly so, as the bold sprays of bloom may be arranged i in large vases, while another valuable trait is ' that the blooms last for some time in good con- dition. Of the hardy border chrysanthemums too much cannot be said in their favour. It is pleasing to find that their value is being appre- ciated for the open air garden, and that a fine display is possible without any greenhouse or conservatory. Those who grow the chry- santhemum in the garden should not disbud the flowers. The early flowering varieties are far more beautiful when grown naturally. The fine sprays of bloom that these plants, when not disbudded, produce so freely should at once convince readers of their value for the house. At one time only the small flowered pompons found a place in the garden, but now the Japan- ese sorts have largely taken their place. Dowdy colours are things of the past, and we now have varieties bearing orange, orange yellow, crimson, and white, with many intermediate shades.

div.head: PLANTING POTATOES.
div.p: PLANTING POTATOES.

There are but very few districts in this coun- try where it is safe for the potato growths to be through the soil before the end of May or early in June. This being so, what ad„vantage is there in planting, say, in March, as is very often done? Planting should not be commenced before the middle of April, and any time be- tween then and the first week in May will answer very well. The disadvantages of early planting are many. In the first place the soil, if heavy, gets so beaten down by the rains that the surface gets hard, and the- young shoots have a difficulty in finding their way through. The surface soil cannot be t& loose and friable, as the looser the ground is the more even in size are the tubers.

div.head: ASPIDISTRAS.
div.p: ASPIDISTRAS.

• These may be grown for several years in the same pots, but there comes a time when the soil becomes exhausted, and repotting has to be done. If this is not attended to, the growths find their way over the edges of the pots, and the leaves assume an unhealthy appearance and split. This is the best season for repotting. If the plants are very large they should be broken ,up, and to lessen the labour in doing so we have found it a good plan to wash away all the sour and inert soil, as in this way it is very easy to disentangle the roots by simply pulling them apart, without having recourse to the knife. A good compost is a mixture of fibrous loam with a little leaf mould or peat and plenty of silver sand. We always use now only the fibrous parts of the loam, after shaking out all the finer particles. This we tried some years ago, and were so pleased with the handsome ,foliage resulting from this compost that we have continued the same treatment. Of course, it must be understood that silver sand was added freely to the soil used. The greatest care is necessary after repotting with regard to water- ing, as if too much moisture is given before the roots are running freely in tno n;w compost the soil will be soured and the plants sullen

div.head: SWEET SMELLING FLOWERS.
div.p: SWEET SMELLING FLOWERS.

How often do we find that many people, in filling their flower beds and borders, quite ignore the sweet smelling ,flowers, only giving place to those that are gaudy and bright?l What more pleasing than to visit the garden of one who, recognising the value of fragrance, grows the night scented stock, mignonette, the sweet scented tobacco, sweet peas, roses, carna- tions, pinks, and the old-fashioned rocket, only found in out-of-the-way cottage gardens? In the house, too, such fragrant flowers as the above are appreciated, while for the sick room what-is- more valued than.a,vase filled with such flowers as diffuse fragrance. Those, then, who value ,fragrance in the garden should, now that the time is with us, not forget to include some of the plants mentioned above, more especially those of annual duration, as the first five men- tioned in the list. Some of the old-fashioned sweet scented pelargoniums may also find a place, and these, if planted out towards the end of May, will help to fill the flower basket with shoots of their variously scented leaves.—Wws in "Farm and Home."

div.head: PEAS FOR SMALL GARDENS.
div.p: PEAS FOR SMALL GARDENS.

The number of sorts of peas now offered by our seedsinen is bewildering,tp the amateur, as he finds it impossible 'which to select. The only redeeming feature of these long lists is that if they are compiled with care one cannot make a very, serious mistake if he makes a selection 'without any previous experience to 4 help him. Of course, we have the early, mid- season, and late varieties, but when all is said and done there is bUt little difference in the table quality or the podding of the different sorts. There is far more difference in the be. haviottr of the different -Sorts iii a—vdrieti"of soils than in anything else. For this reason, o when d.new sort is being tried in fresh ground, it is well to have two or three sorts Sown in moderate quantities s as to be able to select the one which promises to suit- the soil best. At the same time it is a mistake to rely en- tirely on, new sorts, however much they have been boothed, and to guard against failure do not dispense with old and tried varieties, many of which have stood the test of time, and are yet largely grown. A few years ago I made a trial of a new variety which had been boomed, and was disappointed to find that the haulm reached a height of 31 feet before a single pod was forthcoming.'

A Cautious Farmer. Before a local Tribunal a. vrrl strong appeal was made for a man who was required ,to look after applicant's cows. One of the members happened to ask ,how long the farmer ha'l possessed cows. n "Well, I. haven't actually got them yet, but I have them on offer. I'm waiting •to see the result of this appeal. before buy•ing, them," was the reply. , "And how long has the man been with you?" he was asked. "I am not really employing him until I know he is exempted from service."

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.

"Women: Bakers."• In the opening paragraph in last week's '" Chat and Gossip.' I find one or two state- ments which suggest a supplementary word here. The "scientifically constructed hot chamber" has been successfully applied in the case of more than one ordinary kitchen range that I know of. As for women being obliged by shortage of masculine labour to make bread eithcr at the bakeries or in their own homes, they have in many places been so engaged in each. Over a considerable part of Yorkshire especially, the bread is home made. As for Lancashire, I am acquainted with a, young man who, having been trained in a bakery, went to Blackburn in hope of obtaining employment there for reasons private and personal, and re- turned with a story of failure, the explanation being that women are engaged in the bakeries there, whereas master bakers in the town from which he set forth would not employ women on any account.

Stone-throwing. What was said as to this dangerous but favourite diversion at last week's Juvenile Court brought to my mind a bit of personal experience. One forenoon several years ago, I was on my way to petty sessions, and on turning a corner I received full in the face a stone which a youngster had intended for a companion with whom he had quarrelled. I carry the scar to this day and always shall; but, of course, I might easily have been blinded. The Chief Constable apparently, thinks schoolmasters might help to stop this sort of thing.; anyhow, I deem it hopeless—and certainly with reason-- to appeal to parents.

On Tree-planting. tast week's "Farm and Garden "paragraph on The need for raising trees" sent me in thought again to the Rossendale Valley, where, as I noted on a previous occasion, the Bury and District Joint Water Board, which has some 5.000 acres of gathering ground thereabout, has developed a remarkable forest-making scheme. It must now be six or seven years ago since the experiment was entered upon; some 100,000 trees were planted under these auspices, including fir, spruce, poplar, birch, alder, ash and larch; and there have been systematic additions at suitable intervals meanwhile. It may be com- mended to authorities'similarly situated else- where, being calculated not only to increase the beauty of the scenery, but to attract water to the reservoirs. Ultimately, moreover—ani this is a consideration of growing importance— revenue vrill:be derivable from the. timber thus raised at comparatively little expense. Larch Sawfly Pest. This, of course, is an enemy to be dreaded by those interested in afforestation. I well remem- ber that it did tremendous mischief in the country a few years ago, in Cumberland and Central Wales partic,ularly. In a report by the Board of Agriculture it was suggested that the prevalence of ithe pest in those regions especially was due to he circumstance that the woods there consist almost entirely of larch, while in other places, where broad-leaved trees are also planted, birds which devour the larva, of the saw-fly breed in suffie.ent numbers to keep down the pest. The saw-fly had for a number of years been kept in check; then, from some unknown reasons, the delicate balance between the fly and its enemies was upset, and the former increased enormously with disastrous results. Balance of Nature.

This brings us back to what is implied by the familiar phrase, used by "An Old Farmer" in a", letter quoted last week, "the balance of Nature." That the spread of sleeping sickness in Africa has some relation to the demand of fashionable ladies for millinery plumes was a while ago argued by a letter from Sir Harry Johnston, the great traveller and naturalist, the main contention being that with the slaughter of certain birds the various germ-spreading in- sects (like the tsetse fly with its germ of sleep- ing sickness) increase in 'number. This was denied, but was easily proved.

A Word for the Wasp. • • k The wasp is everywhere regarded as a common enemy, to be killed on sight. Is it really pos- sible that a good word may be said even for this hated creature? Take the case of the house- wife engaged in boiling fruit (believe me, there is still home-made jam here and there in these counties). Thitherward, by unerring instinct, the wasps pursue the noiseless tenor of their way. In the height of the season they loot the sweetstuff shops in the like shameless fashion. Besides, they destroy a certain proportion of growing fruit, and producers, along with bee- keepers, have done their utmost to encourage a war of.. extermination, in consequence. My point is that fruit-growers would be worse off if there were no wasps, as- these, troublesome, as they are in some respects, undoubtedly- dbstroy millions of caterpillars and other insects that would otherwise work havoc on the fruit trees.

Helpful Insects. There are insects, as well as many birds, that positively help the gardener in his warfare with aphides, and should, therefore, be carefully pre- served. Of late years I have very, rarely seen a ladybird—a beetle which in the larval stage feeds on aphides, but may then be ignorantly destroyed as a noxious grub. The hawk-flies, at the like early stage, may be mistaken for small caterpillars, yet they devour immense numbers of aphides. The same is true of the grubs of the lacewing flies. Other insects which should not be destroyed are the ichneumon flies, which lay their eggs in the caterpillars of the white cab- bage butterfly, and thus very, materially reduce the numbers of these pests. • I imagine the use- fulness of the ichneumon to be fairly/ well known. For myself I first learnt of it from 'a book by that industrious and enthusiastic, if not very profound,paturalist, the Rev. J. G. Wood. a copy of which was Presented to the when at the age of 1,5, after three years in a solicitor's office. I joined the staff f a newspaper.

Apprenticeship. The incidental allusion to this at last week's meeting of the Trades Council recalled a com- prehensive review of the subject which appeared in these columns some time ago. Of course, I am not about. to, reproduce. any of that able article, but the reference reminded me of some- thing else. In the course of a meeting at Burslem during a wages dispute, one an com- plained that a local firm employed apprentice, who are fifty years old, and another speaker remarked that he had known cases where the father was an, apprentice and the son a journey- man. About the same period a member of the Education Committee of the Wandsworth. Borough Council conceived a scheme for the re- establishment of the apprenticeship system on modern lines, and it was brought before tha London County Council and the City Corpora- tion. The originator's contention was that a great deal of money was paid away in scholar.- ships by the L.C.C. for what he called literary or clerical accomplishments. But there were no scholarships for handicrafts. Now, instead of paying away money for literary or clerical work, if a portion was directed towards defraying pre7, miums to masters for apprenticing boys and girls •to trades, it would be a distinct advantage not only to the young workers, but to the trade of London generally. Perhaps after in this, as in much else, the industrial provinces can give the Metropolis points.

div.head: F.111:11 LABOUR SUPPLY. Complaints From The Warring ton
div.p: F.111:11 LABOUR SUPPLY. Complaints From The Warring ton
Dlstriet Farmers.

At a meeting of the Lancashire War:Agricul- tural Committee," it. Preston , on -119.TR14Y, on tha motioii.-Of- the Warrington. Branch, the :opinion was expressed that the taking of men from the land would result in a serious diminution of the area under potatoes and root crops, and, there- fore, a lack of food for the people. Further- more, it would cause serious disorganisation in the creppiiig (irOtatiots),!. and 'much *land would in -c,onsequence become derelict.. . It was resolved: "That in the opinion of this committee there is already an insufficient sup- ply of agricultural labour ,but if there are cases where this might be reduced, it could be brought about best by friendly arrangements between the farmers concerned." , - • •

The committee protested in the strongest pos- sible terms against the present "arbitrary and unjust method of purchasing hay.and straw, and trust that the Board of Agriculture would take immediate steps to protect farmers in the matter. Furthermore, they fail to see why farmers should be singled. out from all traderd for such unjust treatment.". .

div.head: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
div.p: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
In the Land of Penn, Hampton,
Milton and Disraeli.

The old-world county of Buekingharashire possesses many charms peculiarly its own. There is an undefinable something about its lanes, its villages, and even its small market towns—for there are no large towns in the whole county—which render it particularly attractive. I was staying with a friend re- cently, who is resident in the district, and this is the route he took me through what he well described as "Beautiful Buckingham "—even in these days before the trees are yet in leaf : Amersham to Beaconsfield, 5; High Wycombe 61; Princes Risborough, n; Great Kimble, 2; Aylesbury, .61; Tring, 7; Chesham, n; Chenies, 41; Rickmansworth, 31; Denham, 71; Chalfont St. Peter, 6; Amersham, ; total, 69 miles. Amersham is a quaint little village, which the ravages of time seem to have passed by unscathed. High Wycombe, 'the centre of the chair industry, is not particularly attractive in its modern parts; it possesses many old buildings, however, dating from the 15th century. On the road to Princes Risborough, a few miles from High Wycombe, is the .village of Bradenhatp, the home of Disraeli. The, church of Bradenham has a Norman doorway, commonly supposed to have been built by Swarthy, the Saxon owner of the manor. Monk's Risborough is, perhaps, the prettiest village in the county. Its old cottages are quite a remarkable feature; so are its church and picturesque rectory. Great Kimble will always be associated with one of the greatest 'Englishmen—John Hampton. He was lord of the manor, and it ' was in the parish church that he refused to pay his share of ship money levied by the King. Aylesbury has some fine old buildings, while Tring, a few miles farther on, is the home of Lord Rothschild. The road from Chesham to Rickmansworth, via Chenies, is down the valley of the Chess, where there are some lovely views. The two Chal- fonts—Chalfont St. Peter and Chalfont St. Giles—are well worth visiting, as they are the home of the Quakers; while in the latter village is the house where Milton lived for many years, and where he wrote some of his greatest poems. The old Quaker chapel— hidden away in the woods—and the house of William Penn are in an excellent state of pre- servation. Broadly.ispeaking, the roads ,are fairly good and the hills are never of a nature to cause serious worry. Buckingham is a county that might well have more attention from the wandering tourist.

Some Advantages of the Tandem. A few years ago the tandem was a much more common sight than it is to-day. What the tandem certainly does is to levdl up the relative strength of both riders, a common disadvantage of single machines where the pace must always be that of the slower if there. is to be no lagging behind. For nervous indi- viduals the back seat of the tandem has many advantages, particularly in busy thoroughfares. One thing necessary for comfortable tandem riding is a suitable gear; the ordinary gear is generally too high for average riding. For a lady-back machine about 64 is sufficient, but the best thing is to have a good three-speed gear with a normal 66 to 70. There is a swing about a tandem so fitted that makes it one of the most enjoyable experiences in cycling. Sparking Plug Points. _ _

A 'pump clip clipped. on to the frame of a' motor cycle just above the cylinder is handy for holding the plug when you need to test the spark.. Make the clip a permanent fitting and , It will always be there when you want it. Guaranteed plugs, which the makers will re- place free of charge in the event of troubk over -a stipulated period, are the ,cheapest in -the-long run., The initial, expenditure repre- sents the total expenditure on 'plugs over the period covered by the guarantee. Choose a plug with good, strong, thick insulation. A motor cycle plug has to withstand enormous • pressure. Frequently clean the points with a tooth-brush dipped in petrol. Never allow a carbon deposit to form on them. Always have the lock-nuts on the shank screwed up tight. Never carry a. "dud" plug as a spare. Take in your tool bag something on which you know you can absolutely rely. One advantage pos- sessed by the plug with a single point over a plug with two or more points is that the risk of one of the points coming adrift and falling into ,the, cylinder .is 'reduced to a minimum. A plug placed over the inlet valve keeps 'cleaner and cooler than one placed over the exhaust • valve, and, therefore, retains its efficiency longer. Have the points of 'the plug set at the correct distance apart, 1150th inch. This. spells easy starting and correct :firing at all. speeds.

Petrol Consumption and Two-strokes. . In the early days of two-stroke engines it was regarded as quite an achievement to get them to two-stroke at all. The question of spirit con- sumption and thermal efficiency was not con- Siclered. But with petrol at its present iniquitous Price it is another Matter; and there is to-day very common complaint made by users of the two-stroke machines that they can. only average much smaller number of miles to the gallon. The engine is very attractive With its lightness, simplicity, and. suitability .as a ;power unit for a small Mount. Thus it is a great pity that the quantity of petrol used is so excessive. Ido not want to condemn the two-stroke machine, but to render it really effective many improvements are needed. It may be that a special carbur- etter is required. Perhaps .the, position and design require altering, so as, to render this engine as efficient as a four-stroke. Whatever is the cause it is up to our manufacturers to determine it and overcome it, for otherwise it will speedily affect its popularity.

What a Tyre Should Be. The most important requirements of a tyre are rolling efficiency and tractive efficiency, durability and comfort. But another very im- portant feature of a tyre is the grip that it gets on the road, including freedom from sideslips and skidding.. A rubber non-skid will hold on fairly greasy and dry smooth roads; a -steel, studded non-skid will .grip a very greasy road, but fail on a hard polished surface; while a

div.head: BOY RUN OVER AND KILLED.
div.p: BOY RUN OVER AND KILLED.
A Careful Driver.

A seven-year-old boy named Thomas Richar 1- son, son of Lance-Corporal Henry Welsbr Richardson, 214th South Lancs. Regiment, and , of Mary 'Richardson, residing at 45, Wakefield- street, Warrington, was knocked down by a taxi-cab in Guardian-street on Saturday after- noon, and _received such injuries that he died .p.t the Infirmary shortly after admittance. At an itiqUest an -Monday night a Coroner's jury returned a verdict that the boy met his death accidentally, and exonerated the driver of the taxi-cab, Walter Bradshaw, 11, Henry- street, from all blame.

Emily Seninr, 10. Brierley-street, told the jury that about 2.15 on Saturday afternoon she was cleaning bedroom windows, when she noticed a, taxi-cab being • driven along Guardian-street from the Workhouse. Deceased ran out of a, back yard and endeavoured, to cross the street, and was- Caught, by the front of the taxi-cab. Tie was knocked- down, the .rear wheel passing over his body. The taxi was travelling at a ' slow speed and, the driver sounded his hooter 'several times.- _ , Walter Bradshaw; the driver of the taxi, stated that before he had time to apply -the brakes the boy .was knocked down. Ile, removed him with all speed to the Infirmary. The boy was found to be suffering from a frac- tured skull and internal injuries. Witness • had been driving seven years and had never' pre- viously injured anyone. Mr. E. A. White, who represented Bradsha w- and his employers, expressed sympathy with the parents of the deceased, with which the Coroner (Mr. S. Brighouse) associated himself. After the jury 'had recorded: their, yerdi2t, the Coroner said Bradshaw had driven him about, and be ,knew him ,to be a most capable and careful driver.

div.head: ONTARIO MINERALS.
div.p: ONTARIO MINERALS.

According to the Ontario Bureau of Mines, the value of metallic and non-metallic produc- tion for 1915 was $57,532,844, against $46,295,959 in 1914. Of this increase of $11,238,866, $10,588,756 is accounted for by the nickel and copper contents of the Sudbury mattes. In 1915 the gold production was 411,5880 z., value $8,501,391, compared 'with 268,9420 z., value $5,529,767 in 1914. while the silver production was 23,730,8390 z., ;Against 22,243,6840 z.
"LOWERING THE SCHOOL NE."

div.head: Restrictions On Exemptions.
div.p: Restrictions On Exemptions.

At the Education Committee meeting on Monday night, the following letter was read by the Director of Education from: Mrs. S. Jones, 52, Willis-street, secretary of the Women's Co- operative Guild, Warrington Branch : " Dear Sir,—The following resolution was moved at the above branch on _Wednesday, April sth:

"That the 'members of • the Women's Co- oPerative Guild deplore the growing tendency tO lower the school -age of children with its Proved ill-effects on health and intelligence and the threatened curtailment of educational facili- !ies. They also point out the difficulty ,of secur- 'l4 good home conditions owing to the increased "mployment of women in industrial life, and therefore call upon the Board of Education to Safeguard the children.'" No action was taken on the letter.

Mr. E. Plinston, as chairman of the School, Attendance Committee, moved the confirmation Of a set of resolutions passed with regard to the granting of exemption from school of chil- dren between 1.3 and 14 years of age. The first dealt with the notice to be given that applica- tion was to be made for the exemption of a child; the second provided that exemptions be net granted to children who are working in s standard lower than the sixth, except in cases of extreme family indigence; and the third, on the reccimmendation of the Medical Inspection Committee, that consideration of applications for exemption be refused in all cases whereAh,? Children, concerned are suffering from some defect for which medical :treatment has been advised but not obtained. Eitherto, Mr. Plinston explained, they had dealt with exemptions applied for up to the very date of the committee meeting, which had thrown a deal of extra work on the staff and. of course, they could not have the fullest in- formation before thein., As to the standard fixed, that had been brought aboit by the fact that of late there hadlieen a greet increase of cases of children from standard -fire who had been granted exemption out of mistaken syra- Pathy. They found that unfortunately these aPplieations were not due to- need, but to thr? Mere fact that the ehildreti" lihd put in just the number of attendances to warrant the amlication. The- committee desired to prevent that occurring in the future. Where parents had been advised that their child required inedieal treatment and that advice had not been attended to, they had decided to support the Medical Inspection Committee by refusing to grant such a child exemption if applied for. even if the other obligations had been met. Mr. Geo. Walker seconded, and it .was carried.

div.head: HOW TO MANAGE WITH LESS
div.p: HOW TO MANAGE WITH LESS
SUGAR.

In face of ,the rise in price of sugar, there *lrises the 'question of management in eeonomis- inZ it. There are several ways in which this ten be done. in the. days.pf peace and, plenty took was given a free hand with the sugar. -140ok at the cookery books, and you will find that the majority of sweet dishes were over- eweetened. None of us will find difficulty in remembering puddings and creams so highly oetened that the flavour of fruit or some other Pleasant ingredient was quite obscured. But we must now deal with the sugar with a light hand. Our palates and those of the children will soon adapt themselves to the reduced sweet- -"fling- Sugarless tea has long been in vogue in the well-to-do classes of society. Let everyone join in and make it universal. The working ,classes may be left out of this crusade—they lik plenty.' of sugar in their tea, and present cir- eumstances they can afford to pay for it. Again 'we may choose for the sweet course such fruits and,jams as are sufficiently sweet in themselves. Their price is sure to go up, but here, too, we must remember that we are paying for sugar as Well ,as fruit. Prunes, for instance, when Properly cooked, are sufficiently sweet to need 210 sugar. Almost an cookery books give sugar as a necessary ingredient in cooking prunes. This is a fallacy. One recip.e has it: "Add 4oz. of sugar 'to 11b. of prunes." Again, "Sweeten the prunes to taste." Well, dear readers, such retommendations belong to the old regime of o*er-sweetened dishes. We must work ourselves out of it as quickly as possible and 'follow ethods more up to date.—" Gentlewoman."

quardians Are Silent. The Officials of Belfast Workhouse have, it is stated, entered upon a " hunger, strike " against margarine, which has been substituted for, bat- ter. They eatAry 'bread instead. *,,Apparently ihe Board of Guardians are content, for they took no formal notice of the complaint,

From these comparatively small beginnings the system of public bake-houses developed gradually but persistently until it reached the state in which we know it to-day. In these times baking bread at home is the exception rather than the rule, and only in the North of England is the custom at all prevalent. This fact may be traced to the historical reason that wood being scarce in that district houses of brick and stone became general earlier than else- where, and the brick bread-oven was therefore not a menace to the dwelling itself. So the fashion for home-made bread is more indigenous to the North than to the South. It now appears, however, that it will have to become fairly general, thanks to the übiquitous labour problem. There are a few of the old- fashioned brick ovens still extant, but the majority of housewives will have to depend on more modern methods of baking their bread. Unfortunately the coal range oven is not at all satisfactory in this respect. The invention of iron ovens with outside heat was due originally to the ingenuity of Count Rumford, who hoped thereby to make all kinds of baking possible in a small house. It was soon clear, however, that the unavoidable variations in the temperature put them out of court as satisfactory bread bakers in comparison with the older type of oven with its gentle and steadily decreasing heat.

So the housewife of to-day who tries to bake her broad in the coal range oven is doomed to disappointment. The coal range, however, is rapidly dying out before the ever increasing demand for gas cooking stoves, and luckily the gas oven, the heat of which can be controlled and reduced exactly the required degree and which is absolutely reliable, bakes bread to per- feetion. .It is merely a question of finding out what particular temperature of the oven gives the best results: the rest is easy.

`Readers will be interested to know that the British Commercial Gas Association, of 47, Vic- toria-street, Westminster, S.W., which has always associated itself with the scientific side of housekeeping on modern lilies, is prepared to send to anyone who applies to the Secretary a special booklet dealing with bread baking at home, which gives full directions and recipes for this useful art.

The thought of making at any rate her chil- dren's bread to help to solve the master bakers' difficulty is one from which no housewife need shrink, for it is by no means a difficult matter under the beet modern conditions. Moreover, bread made at home of good wholemeal flour contains more nourishment and body-building material than baker's bread made from the "best whites" ever does, and thereforelelps to secure those nutritious elements which should be an essential part of the diet in households where the consumption of meat and-egg sis being reduced for the purpose of food economy. div.head: DOMESTIC SERVANTS AS WIVES
div.p: DOMESTIC SERVANTS AS WIVES

Dr. Henrietta Stephens, speaking at Bedford College, said she had seen a great deal of poor mothers during the past ten years, and her experience was that the nice, respectable, superior woman was generally found to have been trained in domestic service. She had had the advantage of seeing the routine of a. good house, where . the children were put to bed early and cared for hygienically, and she had a grip of household things which other mothers of the poorer classes never got. There were, of course, disadvantages in domestic service, and subservience to perhaps a strong-minded 4oman made servants subsequently lack initia- tive.. This came out in the later stage of motherhood, when the child wanted placing out in the world; but they were usually splen- did in managing young children.

Natural Drawing, -
A Touch of Colour.

The Royal Drawing Society is doing good work among children by encouraging individu- ality, and exercising the imagination of artists from eight to eighteen years of age. The twenty-seventh .exhibition held at the Guild- hall was most successful, and the snapshot drawings done by' the, youngest children from memory were quite remarkable. A girl of ten took a prize given, by the Princess Louise, Duchess of Argyll, for pictures of soldiers rid- ing in a training ground. Some caricatures by another child artist were very clever, and gained the bronze star. The portraits were equally excellent. Flowers, landscapes, and animals were also favourite themes; the in- teriors of many churches, too, found favour with not a few of the elder students. But sub- jects connected with the war, with Zeppelin raids, and , aeroplanes evidently exercise a powerful influence on the imagination of the youngest of these artists. Natural drawing, as the method of this society is termed, is a great advance on old-time stereotyped systems.

The touch of colour given to black or dull- toned dresses is not as easy to select, or to place in the correct position, as would appear at first sight. Trained taste is required, first to choose the right colour, then to decide on the amount to be used, and last, but by no means least, to select the position that satisfactorily completes the whole. 'rue graceful lines of a dress are easily marred if the wrong place is selected, but when due attention has been paid to these essentials, the merest suggestion of colour—it may be only a couple of tiny rosebuds—suffices to effectively relieve a dead black toilette. Everywhere this season there is the hint of relief afforded by white or bright colour. Mil- liners and tailors avail themselves of one or the other, or of both. A severe type of tailor-made in navy-blue showed motifs of pastel blue em- broidery, and a dark grey suit was brightened by silver buttons. A front of net, lawn, or lace answers the purpose; for a row of tiny buttons, a bow, or a pin-on knot of ribbon can be u.ed to give the colour needed to the suit it accom- panies.

The Advantages of the Child's Jumper Frock. Fashions were never more suited to youth and childhood than they are to-day. The girl in her teens is often angular, and this, and other shortcomings, may be disguised or soft- ened by the full skirts and the dainty flounces and frills of the present modes. Coloured linen, cottons, voiles, shantung, various light woollen fabrics, with Japanese silk, are only a few of the materials from which the expert in chil- dren's clothes creates the most charming ?oat- frocks, coat and skirts, and jumper dresses f:Nr everyday wear. The greater number of the coats and outdoor frocks are liberally supplied with pockets, big and little, to the delight of the wearers. Styles for children are almost as varied .as for their elders, but for utility 'and economy no dress compares with the jumper, which can be adapted to the needs of the child of six. ov to tilos., of the girl o4' +ri't'en. -Pnr the latter this simple style affords scope for change and variety by means of different coloured blouses, and for originality in the braces or bodice. It looks well in all sorts of materials, in linens and cottons, and is easily laundered, and is made without difficulty by even an inexoerieneed amateur dressmaker.

div.p: lIINTS ON lIE ILTII.

Fireproofing Children's Ciothes. There is an easy and efficient method of fire- proofing the clothing of children which every one should know. Many tragedies can be averted. by applying the method to children's play suits, lace curtains, and such other articles of an inflammable nature as may easily come into contact with lire and so cause serious acci- dents. A solution of aminonium phosphate is used for the purpose, says Dr. Charles Pabst. Dissolve one pound of ammonium phosphate in one .gallon of cold water, and a clear solution is formed in which the fabric to be fireproofed should be soaked for five minutes. The garment can then be taken out and allowed to dry, -after which it may be worn with perfect safety, as it is absolutely fireproof until washed or drenched with rain. The solution produces no more harm to the material than would the same quantity of ordinary water. It will keep indefinitely, is non-poisonous, and can be used for several suits.

Food and the Birth-rate. Lecturing in London, Dr. Josiah Oldfield drew attention to the relation between the diet and the birth-rate. He pointed out that during the last 50 years there had been an increase in the meat ration and a decrease in the birth-rate. This was applicable to every country of West- ern Europe without a single exception. On the other hand, the countries which had retained their ancestral dietaries of coarse meal bread, figs, dates, plums, vegetables, legumens, oil, milk, butter and cheese had retained their high fertility rate. These countries were Turkey in Asia, Bulgaria, Roumania, Serbia and Eastern Russia. It was a matter therefore of grave im- portance for England to learn by the experience of all other countries, and to secure increased fertility in the future by a still further reduc- tion in the meat ration of the people and by a substitution for this of milk, butter, cheese, eggs, whole meal bread, furmity, porridge, dried and fresh fruits, nuts, garden vegetables and pulses, with a plentiful addition of oil or nut margarine. Farmers should no longer give their skim milk to the pigs, but should, in the first place, provide a plentiful supply to the children Of the people.
THE BOY WAS ENGAGED.
A certain Edinburgh doctor was something of a ventriloquist, and it befel that he wanted a

boy to assist in the surgery who must neces- sarily be of strong nerves. He received several applications, and when telling a lad what the duties were, in order to test his nerves, he would say, while pointing to a grinning skele- ton standing upright in a corner, "Part of your work would be to feed the skeleton there, and while you are here you might as well have a try to do so." A few lads would consent to a trial, and re- ceive a basin of hot gruel and a spoon. While they were pouring the hot mess into the skull the doctor would make his voice appear to pro- ceed from the jaws of the bony customer and gurgle out, " G-r-r-r-gr-h-uh th.at's hot." This was too much, and, without exception, the lads dropped the basin and bolted. The doctor began to despair of ever getting a suitable help- mate until a small boy came, and was given the gruel and spoon. After the first spoonful the skeleton appeared to say, " Gr-r-r-r-rh-uh that's hot!"

Shovelling the scalding gruel as fast as ever, the lad rapped the skull and impatiently re- torted, "Well, jist blow on it, ye auld bony!" The doctor sat down and fairly roared, but he engaged the lad.

div.head: KIND-HEARTED GIRL.
div.p: A KIND-HEARTED GIRL.

In the Canadian villages robins, buntings, vesper-sparrows, and many other birds were captured and caged and kept prisoners for the music they make, says the author of "My Woodland Intimates." The custom is not per- mitted nowadays, but years ago captured song- birds were among the commodities trundled over the long, weary miles between the outlying "villages and farms and the market stands in Quebec, with glowers and fruits and vegetables and .poultry-yard products conspicuous among the latter expostulating fowls tied by the legs in bunches of half a dozen, with straw hats and maple sugar, and home-made toys, with the whole stock of a market woman's cart. In short, the poor, terrified little prisoners made the journey to the beautiful city set on a hill. No doubt many of the frightened creatures died before the glittering town came in sight, but, unfortunately, others survived, and if not sold were trundled back to await death or the terrors of the next market day. 1 know a woman who often looks back with unalloyed gladness 'to a certain day of her early , childhood, a bright summer morning, on which, ' armed with a generous supply of copper coins, she wended her way to a market-place that lives , now only in Quebec's memories.

11 The coins re-presented—ii-liiii-bstention from sweets and toys, as for months previous the little girl had .been preparing for the season when the captive goldfinches were to appear •on the market stands. A large cage full of the terrified little creatures came into her posses- sion in exchange for the money—not many I farthings apiece were they—but no sooner was the transfer made than, to the liorror of the vendor and the amusement of the bystanders, the child opened the door of the cage and set the prisoners free. It must have been with a lieart as glad and thankful as their own that !she watched them as they flew away from the Inarket-place out towards the region of green fields and freedom.

div.head: WOMAN'S WORLD.
div.p: WOMAN'S WORLD.
CHAT and GOSSIP,.
By MARJORIE.
Careers for Educated Women.

There were women reporters before the war, but as an occupation it has been followed almost exclusively, by men. It is nevertheless suitable. work for members of either sex, and there is now a chance for women to take it up more generally and attain the ,position of a reporter in the House of Commons or the Law Courts. The qualifications are a good general educations high-speed shorthand, ,a clear memory, and facility in reading back the notes. An equable temperament is also a great advantage, for the work has often to be done under difficult and trying conditions. The war is ever widening the scope for feminine activi- ties, and another career for the educated woman is that of hospital almoner. The' training is not expensive or very lengthy. Candidates must serve for about a year and a half in an almoner's office, where they learn the working of the Poor Law, the technique of charitable work, hygienic physiology, and economics. The duties are mainly to help the poor and ailing in obtaining proper hospital treatment and pre- vent the abuse of the out-patients' department by people who can well afford to pay for a doe. tor's attendance. The Children's Friend.

Miss Margaret Macmillan, whose pioneer work for the children of the poor is so well known and has been copied by almost the whole world—Germany included—is with her sister doing a great work at Deptford. The serious drop in the birth-rate of the country makes the care of those born more imperative than before the war. There is, and has been for years, a needless sacrifice of infant life throughout the land. Yet every child saved to grow up means more power. for the country. And this is the motive that inspires Miss Macmillan and her devoted band of helpers. After her ten years', labours in Bradford, Miss Macmillan decided to start a children's clinic at Deptford, where she inaugurated the reforms she had carried out in the Yorkshire city. Parkin Gingerbread. Take lb. flour, Vb. oatmeal, Vb. dripping, Vb. brown sugar, Vb. treacle, 1 dessert-spoonful grounded ginger, a pinch of salt, a little grated nutmeg, teaspoonful carbonate soda. Melt the dripping, treacle, 'and sugar in a.saucepan over the fire, and stir them into the centre of the dry ingredients mixed together in a basin. Stir until well mixed, then bake in a shallow greased tin in a very moderate oven. time to bake, about ' 1 hour. Probable cost, 7d.—" Cookery for Every Household."

• Celery Fritters. Stew the tender white part of celery in milk and water until tender. (It should be cut in neat Pieces of convenient length before stewing.) Let th 3 celery become cold. Put two tablespoonfuls of flour in a basin, drop in the yolk of an egg, and put the white in a separate cup, in which you may beat it. Use the milk in which the celery was cooked to make a batter of the egg and flour, season it with salt and pepper, and a few drops of lemon. Just before you use the batter beat the white of one egg to a stiff froth, and stir it well in the batter; dip the celery in this and fry in hot lard. Drain on paper and.serve very hot. Air in Bedrooms.

If anyone wishes to understand the real character of the air of a close bedroom, let him get up at five on one morning and just walk out into the garden, take half a dozen deep inspirations, and then come back to his room and shut the door. I'll say nothing about his subsequent language,'hut 1 know he will learn more on the subject than any manual can teach him. Even the clean, airy wards of a hospital seem stuffy to a patient who has lived out of doors. There can be no doubt at all, therefore, as to the great importance that the night air we breathe. should be pure. MY Dun CHILDREN,— Uncle Ned's suggestion that we should have promotions and titles for the best workers in the Children's Corner has found favour in many directions, and I have had a fairly large response to my invitation for hints from you as to what the titles should be. Some of you are in favour of military titles, some of royal titles, some of political titles, 'some of sea- faring •4tles, while ,sonle think we should be numbered in classes. I have not been able to make up my mind what to do in this very im- portant matter; for it is important, as it will :be a prominent.feature of the Corner for years to come. As uncle Red will take charge of the Corner again when the war is over, I think I had better consult him before making any definite arrangements. But the best letter comes from an altogether new member, and I have pleasure in awarding her the prize. She is Niece Lily Scarisbrick, 170, Battersby-lane, who attends Wycliffe School. I congratulate Niece Lily upon being the first boy or girl who has joined the Corner and won the prize with her very first letter. She should prove to be a very useful member.
Next Week's Competition.
Next week I wilt leave you to your own de- vices. You are enjoying your holidays, and will doubtless see many interesting things to write ,about. Just write me

A Letter Upon Anything. Most children have some particular subject upon which they can speak entertainingly, and this opportunity should help them to let me know what most occupies their thoughts., The more letters I get the better I shall be pleased. I hope you will all have a hapPy and profit- able holiday. .
Your loving UNCLE JACK.

div.head: Right Petticoat for the Coat-Frock.
div.p: The Right Petticoat for the Coat-Frock.

The coat-frock bids fair to become almost a uniform, and this is not surprising, for it meets a long-felt need. It looks like a dress indoors, yet becomes a coat in the street. It is always smart; its variety, too, both in material and style, is altogether surprising. It will this spring take the place of the tailored coat and skirt, which is perhaps more suited to the autumn than to the early months of' the year. It becomes the middle-aged woman, the girl of sweet seventeen, or the child in the nursery equally well, and has the further advantage of being decidedly an original garment. In soft zab cloth, trimmed with rows of narrov silk braid, set far apart on the skirt to simulate tucks, it is most desirable. In silk a.lorned with flounces and frills, it is delightful, but of course more expensive. A great deal of the success of the coat-frock depends on the choice of petticoat worn under it. A good silk moirette should be chosen, and made with a full flounce, beginning about twelve inches below the hips, where the petticoat fits tightly. Sgme half-

tion is rife in the Western 'Highlands, in the finest air in the world, is simply because this air is never breathed at night, the bedroom" leading out of the sitting rooms and the windows being closely sealed. Such is the perversity of human nature. I wonder if I have written enough to cause one more bedroom window to be open at night? • I think I had better go on a little longer. I said in a previous chapter that we breathe twice as much oxygen at night as by day; it is, therefore, twice as important that the air be as pure at night as it is in the daytime.—Dr. Schofield. •

How to Roast a Piece of Beef. A good many people find fault with a roast, thinking that the cut is of inferior quality, when really the fault is all in. the cooking. The finest sirloin piece could easily be spoiled by careless cooking, and the trouble is not usually a lack of basting either. It is, when the meat is first put into the oven that the mischief is done. A piece of meat for roasting is often dipped into water, and even allowed to-,..spak in water before it is put into the oven.,, This should never be done, because when the meat is put into the oven the moisture ,will start out the juke which shoul remain in the meat. The meat should be wiped with a damp cloth, and sprinkled lightly with salt, pepper, and, ,fl,bur. Some salt and flour should be spririliied Into the bottom of the baking pan also.: The .meat should be put into the dry pan and set into a very hot oven. It is important that the oven be very hot at first, so that a crust may be formed over the meat, and - the juice kept in. When the flour is dark brown, but in enough water to cover the bottom of the pan. . After the meat has become brown it should be basted every fifteen minutes, and lightly sprinkled with salt and flour. A little hot water should be put into the pan as fast as it evaporates. During the last half hour let the water cook almost entirely away. After the meat is taken up, pour off the fat, and add a cupful of hot water. Set it in the stove, and when it boils stir in a thickening of a teaspoonful a flour and four tablespoonfuls of cold water. Let this boil fire minutes, then add salt and pepper to taste, and Strain into a hot dish. If possible, a rack should be used in the bottom of the baking tin,' which raises the meat about 21n. from the bottom of the tin.
