div.head: AMERICAN SUPPORT.
div.p: AMERICAN SUPPORT.
Striking Manifesto By Prominent Citizens.
GERMANY SELF-CONDEMNED.

The fallowing address to the people of the Allied nations has been signed by 500 of the most prominent people of the United States, including 212 presidents of universities and professors, many well-known politicians, governors and ex-governors of States, 32 bishops, 27 judges and distinguished lawyers, and more than 200 of the most distinguished writers, scientists, historians, and business men of the United States:—

div.head: To the People of the Allied Nations.
div.p: To the People of the Allied Nations.
We, the undersigned citizens of the United States of America, send to you, the people of the nations of the Triple Entente and your Allies, this message:—

Our judgment supports your cause, and our sympathies and our hopes are .with you in this struggle. In saying this we are confident that we are expressing the convictions and feelings of the overwhelming majority of Americans. Since the beginning of the present terrible world-conflict there have not been lacking in America individual expressions of ardent sym- pathy with the cause of Great Britain, France, and their Allies, and horror and detestation of the methods employed by the Teuton confed- erates in the conduct of the war. Patriotic Americans, however, while individually in public and in private expressing their views— which have also found voiee abundantly in the daily Press in all parts of the country—have hitherto hesitated to unite in any more formal statement, at first because they looked to the Government to speak, and later for fear of embarrassing the Government in the difficult negotiations growing out of German offences, and in its endeavour to maintain that official neutrality which it has felt impelled to uphold, in the hope that through neutrality it could best support the tottering pillars of inter-
national law, and aid in preserving—to use the President's phrase—" the foundations upon which peace can be rebuilt." Silence No Longer Possible.

The time has come, however, if indeed it has not long since passed, when Americans owe it to themselves to express more publicly and more formally their sympathies and`their judg- ment. Even as we have always held ourselves as a nation free to express openly our sympa- thies with peoples struggling for their liberties, so now we have the duty of at least making clear our solidarity of sentiment with those who are struggling to preserve the liberties of the world and the highest ideals of civilisation. In the face of the great moral questions in- volved, the right solution of which is vital to the whole future course of civilisation, the American conscience cannot remain silent It cannot run the risk of appearing to be neutral- minded without injury to its own integrity and its self-respect. For this reason it seems fitting and needful that American public opinion should receive some more collective expression. The main facts in the controversy have long been before us. The case of the Teutonic Allies, especially, has not lacked fullness of statement. The ablest German publicists and professors have presented the Austro-German contentions with great eloquence. Numerous German documents have been widely circu- lated, and an active, and sometimes insidious, German propaganda has been extensively car- ried on in the United States. The American
judgment has been deliberately formed, and it is based very largely on a study of German documents and of German statements as to the points at issue. Outrages Against Humanity.

The signers of this document are not un- mindful of the great contributions which Ger- many has in the past made to the common treasure of modern civilisation; all of us acknowledge our debt to Germany; many of us have had the advantage of German educa- tion; some of us are of German blood. But the welfare of that civilisation for which Germany has done so much, the highest interests of Germany itself, demand that in this conflict Germany and Austria shall be defeated. We confidently and hopefully look forward to that result.

The invasion of Belgium we regard as a crime which can never be justified. It will remain a blot upon the history of Europe. The con- science of the American people cries out and protests against outrages upon civilisation committed by your enemies, and against their methods of warfare that break the inter- national laws of nations and the moral laws of humanity. The sanctity of treaties, the rights of small nations, the question as to whether militarism shall dominate over civil- sation are all involved in the final decision.

A peace which does not restore Belgium to the Belgian people and to their own govern- ment, which does not give them such • in- demnity as will allow them, so far as possible, to reconstruct their wasted cities and villages and restore again their ruined prosperity, a peace which -does not recognise the rights of the smaller nationalities of Europe, a peace which does not offer some guaranty that such a calamity as the present war shall not recur— a peace which does not ensure these things would be a disaster and not a blessing. It is because we believe that the success of Great Britain, France, Italy, and Russia will mean the restoration of Belgium and of Servia' and the suppression of militarism that we ardently hope for that consummation. In that hope we believe the future of civilisation to be involved.

div.head: MOTHER'S MAGAZINE.
div.p: THE MOTHER'S MAGAZINE.

"Prom Belgrade to Salonica" is the title of a stirring article appearing in the May num- ber of "The Mother's Magazine," which describes the adventures of an Englishwoman, relief worker and interpreter, who escaped from Serbia after the fall of the capital. Her story makes splendid reading, and the other matter in th 4 issue is well up to the same high level of interest. Particular mention should be made of a page signed by the Bishop of London, and beautifully illustrating his request for the. prayers of a million children. A seasonable touch is given by a lively description of "Easter in Italy," while an article on "Motherhood in Shakespeare" deals with an aspect of the work of him whom we are specially celebrating this spring, which should strongly appeal to readers of the magazine. As always, it is very sound and helpful on the many problems of home management and child welfare, in the widest sense of the words, and a number of special pages for the little ones, the home dressmaker, the nurse and the cook, make up what is really a splendid threepennyworth.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, APRIL 22, 1916
THE THREATENED DESASTER.
Every honest-minded Englishman, whose patriotism is measured by his love of country rather than the chances of furthering his own

interests or ambitions, will 'be relieved to know that the political crisis which:threatened us has passed harmlesslysaway. Seldom were, such grave words uttered as those used in the House of Commons on Wednesday by Mr. Asotrrni when he said that the Government had been unable to agree upon the einestion. of recruiting methods; that continued failure would mean the break-up of the Government; and that "the Cabinet were united in believ- ing that such an event would be a national disaster of the most formidable kind." The PRIME MixtsTEß had not in mind the kind of men that could be got together to take the places of the Coalition, of which he is the head; he had in mind the fact that unrest in high places in England would encourage our enemies, depress our Allies, and cause neutrals to lose some of the faith they have in us principally on the ground that we are a hard-headed, practical kind of people, not given to the antics of the less sober-minded races of the. earth. But, grave as the effect of a political crisis involving the fall of the Government would have been externally, internally it must have been worse. For who would have taken the places of the fallen? We can only presume, awful as the prospect appears to be, • .that the A-• men who had schemed the collapse would have so schemed it in order to enjoy the spoils. Let us imagine England at war under Carson, of Irish civil war fame; Milner, the gentleman who advises the Lords to defy the people and damn the consequences; and a great news- paper proprietor, who is an expert on sweet peas, standard bread and soap combines. These men in place of such men as ASQUITH, GREY, and BONAR LAW! It is sufficient 'to make us despair of the future of the race to think that such a possibility could'have been not only in conttmplation, but pushed to such extremes as to' force the PREMIER to make the sensational statement he had to make. That statement was not long in clearing the air. The next day came the announcement that the Cabinet had come to an agreement, and that the • terms would be announced to a secret sitting of the House next Tuesday. According to the Parliamentary correspondent of the "Daily Chronicle" the statement which Mr. AsQuira will make on-the day after the secret session will show that Ministers have decided on the following measures
Compulsory enlistment of young nten o
Retention with the colours of time-expired men.
Removal of the restrictions on Territorials, enabling Territorial soldiers to be drafted into non-Territorial units.
Combing-out of single men from munition works and other employments. Embodiment of attested married men. \

Unattested married men to be given the opportunity of joining ,the Army as free recruits; failing an adequate response com- pulsion to be resorted to.. State provision for the civil liabilities of married men called up.

This is stated to have satisfied all sides to the eentroversy. Only the wreckers will be dis- appointed, but the more they are disappointed the more nearly shall we be approximating to what is right and proper.

div.head: CONSCIENCES.
div.p: CONSCIENCES.

Messrs. Thomas Howard, ;..,Socialist and prominent member of the Tradee Council, and Harold Brandwood have at length got the ex- emptions from military service to which they had a conscientious objection, not because they were medically unfit, as they also alleged, but because they have already been in that military service to which they .have a con- scientious objection! When they kwere in the Territorials, it is true, there appeared to be no danger of war, but it is difficult to see why men who would now 'do anything, rather than handle firearms should at one time have been enthusiasts for military training. For we have to 'remember that it was only the most enthusiastic militarists ,of our youth who joined the Territorials who languished very badly for members. It is a strange turn of the wheel that allows alien's predent "con= sciences" to be saved by the fact, that they have so lamentably self-abused those con- sciences only a few short years ago. It is also strange that they did not take advantage of this technical loophole before parading their new-found consciences in the manner in which they. have recently done, putting the authorities to unnecessary trouble and ex- pense. But, as we have aforetimes pointed out, there are consciences and consciences.

div.head: Easter Offerings.
div.p: Easter Offerings.

The Bishop of Chester is sure that the laity of the diocese will understand and forgive his reminding them, in connection with Easter offerings, that the war brings to clerical incomes no profit, but by the increased price of commo- dities and heavier taxation seriously reduces stipends, which were already in too many in- stances inadecinate and much drawn upon. The war has also placed additional work upon their largely diminished number.

div.head: GOSSIP.
div.p: GOSSIP.
"Eggs is eggs"—except at Easter, when they are chocolate.

• There were no hot-cross buns this year, be- cause the bakers, like enrybody else, are too short of men to deal with anything else than absolute necessaries. But hot-cross buns are necessaries for ,the children at • Easter, and mother has ,had to provide the best substitute she can, even at the expense of neglecting the "hot" and boggling at the "cross."

"Report one hundred words—more if trouble." This was the instruction sent by a London paper to a reporter who was covering a meeting in the South to be addressed by Mr. Charles Roden Buxton. Mr. Buxton told the story to the gathering in the Friends' Meeting House onlionday.

The Friends and their friends who had been invited laughed and evidently thought. the London message had some -sinister meaning in it. But .1 can assure our Friends that it is quite an ordinary kind of , instruction. News- papers are what their readers make them,, and people's love of a row has to be gratified.

'A prize fight makes much brighter reading than—shall I say?—a learned dissertation on the probable effects of tariffs on countries in an hereafter when conditions will prevail that can be only vaguely comprehended at the time of speaking.
While Mr. Buxton and his brother were in the Balkans, about twelve or fifteen months ago, they were fired at by a Pro-German.
There was some•unconscious humour at the hot-pot supper of the Stockton. Heath detach- ment of Volunteers at the Mulberry Tree Hotel on Saturday.

As half-past nine O'clock approached omin- ously a couple of toasts were rushed in, and then the wishes of the Contral,Liquor Control Board weiv manifest in rows of solemn-looking, empty glasses. The next song was "Drinking!" —and it "went down" well.

• It was Primrose Day on Wednesday—a record Primrose Day, I should say, record in the negative sense. Very few persons wore the delicate spring flower. All our thoughts are concentrated .on matters much too tragic to allow us to think of personal decoration, espe- cially of a political kind.

I see the political clubs in various places sent their customary wreaths inscribed "Peace with Honour," and the like, one sent to a London club bearing the words: if` Would that you were here to-day to steer our ship of State." . -

I am no politician, but I cannot help think- ing it is best for him and best for us that he is where he is. We have enough and to spare of strong-minded politicians trying to take a hand in a game where they are not wanted.

Next Saturday the Market will close at ten o'clock instead of eleven—or twelve—and I hope the shopkeepers will keep faith and close, too. If they do not, more than half the value of the reform will have been lost.
On Wednesdays the Market will close at eight, on Thursdays at one p.m., and on other days at seven.

I wish we could get back to the days when things were more what they seem in the Market. It is a decided disadvantage to have yellow oranges, white goods, and the varied complexions of those who deal in them brought to one common state of blueness. One does not care about being blued in this kind of way.

I am told that my last week's gossip about the poor quality of the football seen in recent Rugby Intermediate -League matches caused some comment at Wilderspool last Saturday. The official view is that the football, taking the season throughout, has been of , high .quality, and that the intermediate teams will furnish some good talent, at least for the Combination team. I am glad to hear it.

Th 4 Editor has handed me a letter he has received from a gentleman Ida is interested in the Deaths and Burials Bill, the object of which is the prevention of crime and the ad- vancement of the cause of humanity.

He calls attention to a barrister, who says: "I personally know two gentlemen who pos- sess their own death certificates.'signed by duly qualified doctors, and under which they would have been buried. At a public meeting of the Association for the Prevention of Premature Burial a lady startled the audience by pro- ducing her death certificate, which, after care- ful medical examination, had been given in the belief that she was dead."
I don't know why the Editor has passed on the letter to me, especially at Eastertide. But he is a gentleman with a'grim sense.of humour —or a sense of grim humour. VIGILANT. . •

div.head: 25 YEARS A GUARDIAN.
div.p: 25 YEARS A GUARDIAN.
Warrington Board's Congratula- tions to Mr. A. J. Jolley.

A quarter of a century service on the War- rington Board of Guardians is the proud record of Mr. A: J. Jolley, and at a meeting of the members on Wednesday, he was the recipient of hearty congratulations. Honour was done him by the members unanimously re-electing him to preside over their deliberations for another twelve months, members referring in laudatory terms to his work for the Board.

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell .hoped that Mr. Jolley's "silver wedding" as a Guardian would lead on to a " golde.n wedding," and when that time came he would look as fit and spruce as he did that day. Mr. Jolley returned thanks for his re-election and the kind references made to his "silver. jubilee." Mr. W. Furness was elected to the vice-chair. All the committees were .re-elected, with the addition of the name of Mr. T. Siddeley, who will serve on the committees previously at- tended by Mrs. Collingwood, resigned. Mr. Siddeley tendered his thanks to the Board for his election. '

div.head: EAST WIND.
div.p: THE EAST WIND.

An east wind blew- across the world, and kept The bursting legions of the Spring at bay; Week after week upon its wintry way It wailed, and gentle women woke and wept Amid their pillows, and beneath them crept To hide their tears, for. still from day to day It bore the awful message none could stay, How Death's scythe over Europe's red fields swept

And mowed down millions. cease, That icy wind which slew the waiting flowers, That chilly blast which bit men to the bone? Was Winter's reign eternal, and would Peace No more come smiling to this earth of ours? And 10, the wind died and the great sun shone!
Would it never
'ARTHtrIZ BENNETT.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 22, 1916.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 22, 1916.
CAN WE PUJIISH GERMAJIY ?
Mr. Charles Roden Buxton and The Proposed
Commercial War.

div.head: SUPER-PATRIOTS AND PROTECTION.
div.p: SUPER-PATRIOTS AND PROTECTION.

The Friends' Meeting House, Buttermarket- street, is not very large, but it was well filled on Monday night by an interested audience, gathered for the purpose of hearing Mr. Chas Roden Buxton, of London, deliver an address on "The Proposed Commercial War." Mr. J. A. Ransome occupied the chair.

Mr. Buxton, in a closely-reasoned address, pointed out that the quotations given in the English newspapers of enemy opinion deal almest exclusively with the extremist side, and neglected the moderate side, which Was much more extensive than people in this country realise.

His main contentions were that we cannot set out to punish the General Powers economic- ally, without at the same time, punishing our- selves, and that we cannot give preference to our Colonies without doing an injustice to our, selves and our Allies at a time when we and they will be suffering from the tremendous financial drain caused by the war. An economic war threatened would postpone peace, and the institution of a commercial war after peace had been declared would only embitter our late enemies and intensify the principal grievance, true or untrue they had —that we wished to limit their industrial ex- pansion and so deprive the German working man of the chance cf work. That is the idea, he said, upon which the masses 0 the people in Germany are now being fed to induce them to continue their support of the war, and ex- treme statements made in this country are specially welcomed and made use If for this purpose by the military caste. It was the belief in this economic grievance that I very largely led to the war.

to bear the vast burden of taxation. He co-ald not believe that the expenditure of this country would be much less than £500,000,000 a year, and how the revenue was to be raised to meet that enormous sum would be one of the most burning questions of the time. There would be two broad alternatives. Taxation fell directly

upon the 'higher incomes or indirectly upon all kinds of commodities. A tariff, and especially three different tariffs, offered a very good chance of distributing this taxation over the mass of the people. The taxing of separate commodities would increase the cost of living, and he was not surprised that these who in the past had always advocated what they called broadening the basis of taxation in .order that incomes might be spared were most enthusiastic for a high tariff after the War. It so happens that their patriotic feelings coincided with the in- terests of their pockets.

div.head: VIOLENT 'WHIRLWIND
div.p: A VIOLENT 'WHIRLWIND
CAMPAIGN.
" Super-Patriois " Who Wish To
Reverse All Our Traditions.

Mr. Buxton said we were threatened with a violent whirlwind campaign—a commercial war against the Central Powers. This proposal was difficult to attack because it was so vague; it was not specified exactly what its advocates were after. The most definite form he had been able to discover Was. that put forward by the Presi-- dent of the British Chamber of :Commeree in Paris, which suggested three separate 'tariffs— imperial preference, special, arrangements for our Allies, and a tariff against our enemies. The first two would involve maximum tariffs and the last one a minimum tariff. Here we had a reversal of the historic traditions of this country and Empire. traditions which happened to be connected, like every other British tradition, with freedom and equality. Those who were opposed to those holding his opinion • on these matters seemed to have a peculiar liking for attacking all British institutions that stood for freedom. First of all came the attack upon free speech, then the attack upon free service, and now they had in an equally virulent and intense form, the attack upon. Free Trade and all connected with it. These super-patriots, who were so anxious to destroy the free institutions which were the glory of this country, were the people who talked most loudly about the war being "a war for freedom!" , "I think they are the true pro-Germans," said Mr. Buxton, "because they are aiming at , setting up in our country all those qualities 1 which are distinctly Prussian, or German, and that is not least the case with their commercial !policy." The whole thing was put forward under the influence of passion, and madness, not of reason. At one Of his London meetings a man rushed on the plat-forth; amid great uproar, shook his fist in his (the speaker's face) and said: "Are you prepared to tolerate a single ship carrying German goods coming into the Thames after this war?" The man was shaking with passion, and if he had replied—as he did not think he had the chance—by saying "I don't think we ought to cut off our nose to spite our face," the man would have been more indignant still, and would have I;;nid it was our duty to crush our enemies disregarding the injury we might do ourselves in the process... It 1-..e.s necessary that we should take up this challenge to free com- mercial intercourse and defend our, position not only because it was an essentially British in- stitution, .not • from any leaning ' towards con- servatism, lant because we believed in free com- mercial intercourse in the world: There was a danger of the country being "rushed " into this change. and he for one had never felt any hesitation from the first in opposing it. root and branch. However unpopular it might be, he was determined to stand up against the idea of a commercial boycott after the war.

div.head: WHAT THE GERMANS BELIEVE.
div.p: WHAT THE GERMANS BELIEVE.

The harm these proposals were doing now was great: they were actually prolonging • the war, for under such a threat our enemies would fight more determinedly and would be less ready to submit. The extreme utterances in this country that we wish to 'annex purely German territory did" infinite harm, because it made Germans believe that we were aiming at the destruction of their country, not of their aggressive power, but of their defensive power. That was now universally believed and was con- sidered proof of the theory that we entered.into the War for that • purpose. That might seem ridiculouato us, but it was believed in Germany, and colour was • given to it by those extreme utterances not always made by persons in un- important positions. That class of statement did not affect the working classes of 'Germany so' much as the middle and upper classes.; but it Was different now that this declaration of •a commercial war had been made.. When Mr. Runciman Said we must prevent the economic recovery of. Germany and prevent her , from again lifting up her head, it was put before the working classes of the Fatherland that England was aiming at their destruction. The German Government and the German military caste were able to say to the 'people that it was England's aim to destroy- German trade and so injure the daily life of the German worker. That, of course, had had a most disastrous effect. Such statements were welcomed by the German militarist party for the effect they had upon the people. and they would undoubtedly have the effect of prolonginc, the war. "We have important demands to. nut for- ward," continued Mr. Buxton, "in the interests of small nationalities, and if we are not pre- pared to make any economic concessions on the other side, we shall find it hard to realise the objects we have at heart; and if we are pre- nared not to threaten a permanent commercial boycott "we -shall find it easier to obtain those concessions we wish in the way of nationality."

div.head: COMING IMPOVERISHMENT.
div.p: COMING IMPOVERISHMENT.

If this policy of the boycott were brought into being what would be the effect upon this country? Dealing with the purely economic point of view After the war there would be tremendous impoverishment. The destruction of capital -wealth in this country will have been tremendous; our resources will have diminished vastly; it will be extremely difficult to obtain capital for new industries or for restarting old industries, however much such industries may be needed. That would have a disastrous effect upon the labour market, and it would be diffi- cult to find employment for the vast numbers of men who would be suddenly dismissed from the Army to compete for places, the wages for which would come down. The immediate need Of the hour would be to build up our wealth again, to create new wealth, to increase and maintain our productions. In order to do that we ought to remove every possible barrier from our path. The policy which was put forward would in- crease the barriters and restrictions, diminish new production, would be a drag upon the creation of new Wealth, and we should see the effect of high tariffs. The industries of Lanca- shire and Yorekshire especially, which depend to a very considerable extent upon commercial intercourse with Germany, would be most heavily handicapped. Industrial England Would be severely hit, and our impoverishment would be intensified. We should further have

div.head: PERMANENT PEACE NEEDED.
div.p: A PERMANENT PEACE NEEDED.

However, he. was not sreaking from an economic, but from an int.rnational point of view—of creating conditions thet would not lead to another war. That was the most essen- tial point of view of all. Our relations with our own Allies would be -rendered very much more difficult by a Policy of this kind. An imperial preference involved a tax upon goods coming from France, .Russia and Italy, in order that we might take off some of the charges in the interest. of our Colonies. In the case of wines, Lord Courtenay had pointed out that, in order to give a preference to, Australian wines, we should have to. put a higher tax against French wines just at the moment ,when France will he struggling in the deepest industrial trouble ,sh,? has ever known: ,while she • was struggling to- wards recovery we , were, to deal her this new blow. That was one small example. Difficul- ties between ourselves and neutrals bordering on Germany would be created; but the most important point had reference to trading with those who were now our enemies. In order fully to understand the iniquity of these pro- posals we had to realise what was the special : grievance of Germany and Austria before the I war. Their grievance was an economic one. ' I They thought they had not anything like tha - chance of other Powers of economic expansion; he did not say whether the grievance was true Or false, but it existed and contributed towards bringing about the war. A great, industrious, growing nation saw the greaterpart of the world occupied by other Powers, while their indus- tries were excluded from a great part of it. They occupied a few small specks in the world, and, the rest was pegged out by/those who surrounded them and increasingly occupied them to their exclusion in recent years. If their economic expansion was not merely left where it was but placed within still narrower limits, their grievance would be intensified and their feeling of resentment would be increased tenfold, and the whole people—not the governing classes only —would Concentrate all their energies in break- ing through restrictions set up to restrict their commercial expansion. In other words, we should create just that kind of spirit aria irritation which would lead to the further piling up of armaments and a competition for those spheres of influence which were as yet unsettled in East Africa or elsewhere. There would be increased . suspicion, a pernetuation of war memories and -the creation of an atmosphere of unrest which he was afraid was very -likely to render useless all efforts made in the interests of a, permanent peace. . • - • "We aim at ,ft permanent peace." said Mr. Buxton. speaking • in the •name of • the "We have the utterances., of -many leading statesmen in that matter on -our side. Mr. Asquith and Sir Edward Grey-look forward to better conditions. 'We don't doubt their sin- ' eerity; but how can we hope to have that better international system if,-we /hare poisoned our; relations with, each. other ate very .r,our .e I, for one, feel that it would he of very doubtful value and futile to hope for better international relations if we alio-WM thrs— great economic grievance to be intensified, leaving cne of the root causes of the war as had as, or 'Worse than, it was before the war. That is my main objec- tion to the cominercial war. end We mean tO work in the opposite direction," - AN ATTEMPT THAT CANNOT SUCCEED. This question was wider than the old Free Trade v. Tariff .Reform ContrOyers. Ifwas not the mere negative conservative proposition that this country, ought not to.abandon a Free Trade policy. It was not the business of the U.D.C. at all; but in so .far as the' question. was in- volved it .was 'in the interests of future peace and good relations that ther,, should encourage wherever ''they could the • fallest commercial intercourse, .and that they should fight for th?, , Policy of .the open door, which did not mean Free Trade. It meant that duties should not be -imposed upon one Power that were not im- pose& upon another, and that .areas shOuld not

_ be mapped Out as the exclusive'. preserves of a particular Power. "if we are going to attempt to exclude, 120,000.000 of most industrious , people from some thing like two-thirds of the egtrth's surface, in- cluding the whole of Asia an Africa, we shall be attempting something which will not in the end succeed and which, before its failure has been demonstrated, will have done more than anything else to make peace impossible." The policy of the open door was approved by the reasonable, sober people in every country— neutral and belligerent, and would satisfy them, although extremists might not like it. It was only by unanimity between the different sides that they could secure that stable Deace-for which we were contending. (Applause.)

div.head: MR. BUXTON QUESTIONED.
div.p: MR. BUXTON QUESTIONED.
The Power And The Impotence Of
Tariffs.

• In answer to Mr. Ilansome,'. Mr. Buxton said most countries had lowered their tariffs. since the ivar began, particularly upon foodstuffs. France, Germany and Italy did so; in :some cases the .taxes upon food had been entirely. removed—forced out by the necessities .of the people. He : questioned whether such taxes would ever be put on again. We had to. raise a vast amount of revenue, and our people would .have to resist the pressure which. would be brOught to'hear by a section in this Country in favour of raising it by tariffs. Mr. Buxton, replying to the question whether barriers did really stop trade, seeing that we already did trade With.. countries. with tariffs, including Germany., said tariffs did not stop trade, but .they hampered it.. Our trade with Germany :would have been greater but for the tariff barriers. But what was now proposed wa3 a minimum prohibitory tariff. Mr. Dunlop: Has the proposed tariff its source in the desire to prevent Germany from risin; again? Mr. Buxton: The motives are mixed, but in. The niinds of most who adyocate it is an idea of punishment or somehow or other proving that we won't associate with such people again. That is the kind of idea, and the idea of keep- ing Germany and Austria, permanently weak from a military point of vie*. Of -.course, I. think that will fail—a prohibitory tariff Would only drive the Central Powers:back upon greater measures of internal Free Trade and a Stronger customs union with the -neTitral States.. They are far too industrious, skilful. and energetic not to be able to build up their industries again.

div.head: GERMAN COLONIES.
div.p: GERMAN COLONIES.

Mr. E. England asked whether the German Colonial Empire was so small as Mr. Buxton seemed to indicate " when he described the Colonies as "specks." Mr. Buxton said the Colonies of Germany were only specks in a vast area, as they would see by looking at a marked map of the world. Most of the Powers thought more of Colonies than they ought to do, and exaggerated the advan- tages they got from them. There were some advantages, however—a people with a large oreign trade, assisted by Colonies. were better Ø. than a people who had not. They provided openings for enterprise. " Did Germany practise Free Trade or the
Continued in next colony'.
CAN WE PUNISH GERMANY?—Continued.

policy of the open door in her Colonies?" .asked' another gentleman. : Mr. Buxton: The open • door. There were., no,; higher duties against outsiders than against. Germans. In the French Colonies there is a very exclusive system • against foreigners, in- cluding ourselves. Mr. Buxton, asked whether the successful ex- clusion of Germany from sthe commerce of the world would not make our own case worse, re- plied that he thought it would. The world should be developed to the utmost by the free exchange of commodities, and barriers set up diminished production: If we excluded Ger- many and Austria we Olould no longer be able to Send goods across those countries ,to other 'countries, and the increased cost of transport to us would ,be 'enormous.. \

div.head: WESLEYAN MISSIONS.
div.p: WESLEYAN MISSIONS.
Good Friday Services At Bold
Street Church.
SUCCESS EN WAR YEAR.

The Rev.. Wm. Goudic, of London, was the special preacher at the Good Friday missionary services, held at the Bold-street Wesleyan Church. At the Morning service there was . large congregation,' .Which included a goodly Sprinkling of -Men in khaki. • The Rev. Wm. Goudie took for his subject the experience and ministry of reconciliation, show- ing that from the missionary point Of view they were implicit in all the true discipleship of Jesus Christ. The life of this discipleship, according to the Apostle, began with the ex- perience of reconciliation.- "He reconciliated uS. to Himself -through Christ." • The Apostle had habitually thought of himself in terms of his moral relationship with God, and regarded the one great Outstanding event in his life' the work of reconciliation, which Made him the friend of God, and brought his will into har- mony With the divine will. The preacher insisted that such it broadening procesS was necessary in the minds of the Church of our country. The reason why so ninny people were not reconciled to God was be- cause they did not Come into the Kingdom of God by the way .of God. Recon- ciliation with .God was a wonderful life—beauteous as ft spring morn. It brought them into concord with our Father. Let a man know Jesus Christ he could never be narrow- minded and bigoted again.

div.p: SATISFACTORY REPORT.

The reverend gentleman reported that despite the difficulties caused by the war, the Society had this year paid its way, and wiped off the deficiency for previous years. The Warrington Branch contributed £336, made up as follows ;--Bold-street, £4l us. Id.; Bewsev- road, £23 12s. Penketh, £B3 15s. 3d.; Moore, £2l ..17s. 10d.; Antrobus. £l3 Os. 7d.; Whitley. £6 Bs. 10d.; Appleton, £8 25.; Padgate, £3B 7s. Bd.; Martinscroft, £ll Os. 6d.; Stockton Heath, £l6 135.; Winwick, E,l 11s. 3d. This was an increase for the Circuit of £l9 11s. 10d. There was also a decrease of £5 14s. na. in expenses. so that the net increase was £25 16s. ld. The Bold-street Society showed in- creased subscriptions of £1 us. 4d.

div.head: BROKEN AWAY FROM CIVILISATION.
div.p: BROKEN AWAY FROM CIVILISATION.

The Rev. W. Goudie, in his evening address, spoke of missionary work from what he described as a fresh point of view. They had to look at it from the point of view of Christianising the civilisation of the world, an aspect Which should carry weight at the present time, when we recognised that all the sorrow, loss and dread which laid upon us heavily to-day, was due to the fact that the great -civilisation across the. North Sea had broken away from the religion of Jesus Christ and had built up a political system, from which. good had been largely ex- cluded.

In regard to India and China it was import- ant for the moral well-being of the world that they should see to it that the civilisation, which those countries were seeking from the West should have as its most dominant istfluence that faith which had hallowed the life of this country for 2,600 years_ Dealing with the position in Africa and the negro population, the reverend gentleman spoke of the negro's remarkable capacity for handling money, accumulating wealth, their strong desire for education, their social, racial and political combination. In the near future they would be dealing with great masses of black people, moved with one common ambition, co-ordina- tion of their resources of education and wealth for one common end, and cherishing one .deep jealousy—jealonsy of the white man.

div.head: REV. H. OGDEN WANTS TO KNOW.
div.p: REV. H. OGDEN WANTS TO KNOW.

The Rev. 11; Ogden felt that the purpose 'of this commercial war was not so ranch" a question of trade IA of punishment, and he found him- self endorsing Mr. -Buxton's fear that this "punishment," instead of laying the, founda- tions of peace, would sow the seeds of another war. But was it .not a fact that all tbe com- mercial prosperity of Germany, all her existence as a commercial force, were subordinated fo her military. methods? If there had been some kind of restrictions'on her trade would it have been possible for ,Germany to have laid by the enor- mous- preparations she evidently had at the moment of war?-

"I• am alarmed." said the reverend gentleman, "at what may follow from a commercial war, but I am also concerned to know how Germany may be moved to a better spirit or prevented from piling tip her strength against another 'day.' How do you suggest that German/ should be brought to a better state of mind?"

. Mr. Buiton said he had never seen any proof that all Germany's commercial development hAd been subordinated to military or semi-militqc y ends. He did npt believe it was true. He had an open mind; if anyone could .bring evidence that he was wrong he wortld be prepared to accept it. The idea was to impoverish Germany which meant • lowering ..the standard of the people. It Was bound to fail: it was impossible to impoverish a • whole • people. The attempt would only drive them towards revenge - "How high would the 'tariff barrier have to be to keep Germany out?" asked, a gentleman in the audience. . Mr. Buxton .said it was doubtful. Germany had great powers of organisation. and all sorts of ways could he 'found of getting round tariffs.. Many people. including Englishmen,. got tound them by establishing businesses'in the protected countries.

Mr. W: IT. Sherburn : 'Would it be.. to the in- 'terest. of the working classes if .in order to sur- mount the . tariff, impositions, industries were transferred from one 'country to. another? • Mr. Buxton: It depends on the character of the. enterprise. If; they were genuine enter .prise and the distribution of wealth anything like fair, the whole system would be good.
"JUDGE NOT

: Mr. Lloyd jones asked: Supposing the punish- ment policy was attempted: and suceeeded, in what terms would Mr. Buxton characterise that policy from the high Moral point of view? Mr. Buxton: I don't believe one nation can Punish: another. No punishment can be effective unless- it produces- some effect on the mind of the' persOn to be punished, and I can- not see any proposal which would produce any improving effect upon the mind of Germany. Some people, are so simple as to believe that if the Ger Man people are crushed they will change their opinions of u and deeide that they have been wrong. On .the contrary, it would only intensify the opinion they have . Person- ally I believe the divine truth '" Judge not that you be not judged." I never discovered until this war the profoundest truth that underlies that phrase. I believe it to be not only a just utter- ance, but also the Profoundest reason and common sense; and while I believe there is such a thing as justice—divine justice if you will, and not to be carried out by human agencies-- we are not in a position of an impartial judge to survey the whole of humanity and deal out justice. I think it a great mistake to cherish any such idea. Mr. Sherburn. proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Buxton, said be had given them a states- ludnlike exposure of a most shaniefut. attempt to get behind the party truce by people wha hoped to get something they could not get by any other means. M. Harold Gray seconded the resolution, which was heartily carried.

div.head: An Alderman on Wisdom.
div.p: An Alderman on Wisdom.

The Rev. T. T. James presided on Sunday' at a well attended meeting of the Wyeliffe.P'.S..A., when Alderman 'Hunter, of Leigh, spoke. on ".. Wisdom." Wisdom, said the Alderman, had always been needed, and was 'now needed more than ever. If the nations of Europe had exer- cised wisdom this dreadful conflict would never' have taken place. 'Religion did not save .us from war. Germany .was greatly. religious, but wisdom was not to the front. Daily life, family life, needed' caution, tact and wisdom.. We should not be carried away with being "straight' which was rudeness-.'- Mr. McEachern and Mr. B. Fararr took part. A vote of sympathy was passed with Councillor James Shaiir, whose son has been killed in action.
Dardanelles: Coming Red Cross
Lecture-:

In another column ig advertised particulars of a lecture to be given at the Parr Hall next Saturday .b.T Dr. John, Grimshaw, of Liverpool, on his experiences during a visit to the Dar- danelles.' This lecture is arranged by the Brit- ish Red Cross. Society, .and the entire proceeds will be divided between the Prisoners of War Pond - (South •Laneashire Regiment and the British- /ted Cross 'Society. • We hope that Warringtonians will give their hearty support to such good 'objects. We can assure them that the lectnre will be one of ab- sorbing interest.. It is illustrated by over 90 limelight views of photographs taken by the lec- turer during the time he spent with our gallant troops.

. . Frodsham Auxiliary Military Hospital. Mr. •Holnian Kingdon arranged a delightful concert for the entertainment, of the wounded soldier in the above • institution on Tuesday afternoon, the artistes being. Miss Marie Hough- ton and Messrs. Miss Marie Houghton sang a number of songs, which so pleased the audience that she had to respond to double encores. Mr. Lambert was very. Successful with his recita- tions, coster character songs, and humorous songs. Mr. Jones has a very pleasing voice, and happily chooses songs which please the wounded warriors So that altogether the soldiers thor- oughly enjoyed themselves, and heartily joined in the choruses of the songs they knew. div.head: Russian Order for Leather.
div.p: Russian Order for Leather.

• The' -Warrington Correspondent of the. "Leather Trades Review" says:—There has been a great deal of speculative bnYing.here dur- ing, the past week: and, from' the number of buyers again in the district,, it does not show any signs of slackening; in fact, tanners have been inundated with inquiries regarding the great Russian order, which, I understand, is to be given out during the next few days, and then what a rush for leather during the next three months! _lt will certainly put •0,6 tanners to 'very high pressure to enable them to cope 'with the demand for bends and shoulders between now and the end of June; but mhat the ordin- ary trade will do in the meantime I do not know, becimAe every ounce of leather pro„iluced, other than light and damaged bends, will be taken up for this gigantic order,

div.p: Time-Expired Soldier-Teacher.

He was sure the Committee would welcome him back to their service now that his time had expired, and, while recognising the services he had rendered his country, -would express their satisfaction that he had returned 'sound in health and limb. • • The Chairman said all would agree with the sentiments expressed by Mr. -Upson. •

div.head: Good Friday Service at 'Wycliffe.
div.p: Good Friday Service at 'Wycliffe.

The Rev. T. T. preaching A Wycliffe, yesterday, dwelt on the permanence and last- ing power of the Cross of Jesus Christ. In the days of the decay of the Roman Empire, when men and women were sated with the material pomp and pageantry which was already fading into nothing, and when the tramp of bar- barian hordes could already be heard at the gates. of the Eternal City, there . were those who gave the impression by the light in their eyes and the beauty in their lives of a secret of a lasting and enduring nature. When Rome Crumbled into dust and became a Memory the Cross stood in the centre of the This,was the comment of history upon the story of the Gospel; amidst the rise and fall of nations, the shaking and tottering of thrones, the prosperity and decay of peoples, the one thing that lasted was the Cross of Christ. Out of the dead. past .there came this riving thing; out of the changes and viciSii- tudes of history there came the changeless -force, in the lives of men. We came to .the Cross,' because there have been said the best things about God and about men, the best things about life and about death. We come to it because without it there is so little that we know, and with it there is so little that we need fear. ' Hymns from Stainer's "Crucifixion" were „ . . sung at the service. There was a large congre- gation. Last Sunday evening Stainers cantat .".Crucifixion," was rendered by the Wycliffe 'Congregational Church Choir, the Rev. T. T. 'James conducting the !service, but omitting the :sermon. Mr. Joseph Poole (tenor) and Mr. F. E. Brown were ,the principal soloists, the minor [solos being taken by Mr. Arthur Davis, These I gentlemen and the chorus acquitted themselves very creditably. Mr. W. IL Payton was at the organ. The offertory was on behalf of the choir funds.

div.head: Red Cross Finances.
div.p: Red Cross Finances.

The annual report. of the Daresbury Division of the Cheshire branch Of the British Red Cross Society makes good reading, showing as it does that the society is being well supported locally, and that its work is being-well administered by those in 'authority. In- the .accounts for the year 1915 the receipts amount to 4:2,298.195., the balance in hand being .0t254 12s. Bd., against £241 is. 3d. brought forward. from the preced- ing year. Of this A:2;298, no less a. sum than .4,976 17s. Bd. was expended upon. the mainten- ance of Haddon Court Hospital, the only hospi- tal run by the division. The only other ex- penses were: Meetings and lectures, .43 95., tid. ; stationery, telegrams . and sundries, £2l 18s. Wid.; material for working parties, A:26 10s. 3d.; contribution to county hind, ..25; and donation to National Union of Trained Nurses, 10s.

General donations to the funds anfounted to £656 Cs. 7d.; entertainments produced £146 13s. Bd.; members' Subscriptions amounted to £22 is., and associate& subscriptions to £7 155.; old Government grants to the hospital produced £1,158 Bs., the allowance being 2s. per patient per (lay, not an extravagant amount, consider- ing that the men received at the hospital are being built up during convalescence upon a plentiful and nourishing diet. Pound days pro- duced gifts in kind valued at £7O. The details of the cost of running Itaddon Court Hospital are advertised on our front page by the hon. treasurer, the Rev. G. C. Briggs. It will be noted ;that whereas the amount re- ceived by the hospital from the divisional funds is £1,976 17s. Bd., the total receipts at the hospi- tal were £4,151 119. 70. Provisions cost £1,077 12s. 9d.. The other items, will be found in the advertiseinent, but it :May be Mentioned_ that the hospital had a balance in hand on the year's working of £174 13s. 11d.,..• • Mrs. Oliver Wheeler, Whitecroft, Stockton Heath, the hon. secretary, has asked us to say that it: is hoped. all supporters will accept, Ihrongh this medium, the thanks of the officers and Committee for their generous and welcome help, without which the :work of the Red Cross Society—constantly increasing •in • all its branches while the war lasts--could not be car- red on.

div.head: SCENE IN A TRAIN.
div.p: SCENE IN A TRAIN.
Warrington Soldier And Man- chester Merchant Fight.

A. Manchester merchant named Robert Edward Parkinson, of Mamie House, Flixton; and Private Herbert Fallas, of .the stationed at the Warrington War Hospital, were summoned on Tuesday at the Manchester City Police Court for interfering, with the com- fort of passengers on a Cheshire Lines train. The prosecuting solicitor stated that the two Men were passengeis in a crowded carriage of a train from the Central Station, Manchester. A- remark by Parkinson and a retort from Fallas were followed by blows. 7 Other passen- gers in the carriage were knocked about in the: course of the disturbance, and the train was stopped and the men's identities ascertained. ,A number of passengers gave evidence, in- eluding three ladies, all of whom declared that Parkinson began the trouble by addressing the soldier in an offensive manner. In reply to the Magistrates, Parkinson said he honestly believed that, Pallas had had more drink than was good for him. • That was the reason he gave utterance to the Observation, "You are a fine specimen to wear thast/ badge on your arm; you are a disgrace to the society to which you belong." Fallas thereupon re- plied, "What are you doing in `civies'? Who are you?" ,
After a long hearing the magistrates dis- miSseil the summons against Fallas, and fined Parkinson one guinea. They also ordered him to pay Ms. extra costs.

div.head: TRIBUNAL'S DUTY.
div.p: TRIBUNAL'S DUTY.
13 Held The Balance Justly In
Appeal Cases.
FARM LABOUR SHORTAGE.

Mr. J. Ball, a member of the Warrington Rural istrict Tribunal, at a meeting of that body on Wednesday, took up the question of Aihortage of labour on farms, and *wanted to know. if the Tribunal were to continue with the same grounds for refusing exemptions to farm labourers as before, or if any fresh orders had come thratigh. The Chairman (Mr. Mather) said it was a question Mr. , Ball ought not to ask. The Tri- I)unal was there to represent those outside; the :wilitary representative the military. Mr. Ball said Lord Selborne had stated that no pair of horses must be robbed of its driver, ;and no bailiff should be taken, and lots of ()tiler things. The Chairman: We are here to judge between cattle and cattle. We are the Tribunal to ettle these, cases. Mr. Ball said if they did not consider the :requirements Of the country they were of not much use.

The Chairman replied as individual members of the Tribunal they must work on the lines they thought best. Mr. Ball, continuing, said he was not speak- ing as a farmer, or in the interests of farmers, I)nt in the interest of the nation. During the Past four or five months War Agricultural CommitteeS had been established, whose sole Object was the production of food and the good illtivation of all soil. That must show that the Board of Agriculture was not altogether Batisfied with the work of the Tribunals, inas- lunch as they had asked that a representative should be appointed on the Tribunal. He com- plained that men who 'proposed to speak authoritatively on this matter knew absolutely nothing about it. The Chairman: What the Tribunal is for is to ,hold the balance. We don't control any other Tribunal but this: We are a' judicial body to mete out justice to any appellant who comes before us. The military representative is to look after the military side. The agricul- tural community is to be represented- to look after their side. We have not to be led by Tribunals in other parts of the county, but do our duty conscientiously and fairly. That is as far as we can Mr. Ball remarked that the general public were fond of saying "hi is a farmer, with one or two sons; why cannot he spare one?'" but when a man had five or six sons in munition 'works nothing was said about it. The Chairman: You are in a judicial capa- (•ity and you •should not listen, to what other People say. I think this discussion is irrevelant ,and ought not to have taken place. Say what you have to say about each appellant when the case comes forward.

div.head: FIFTH SON TO GO.
div.p: FIFTH SON TO GO.

The Tribunal had only a few appeals to con- sider. A Penketh young man, • who appealed en the ground that he materially helped his mother, said he had already four brothers in the Army, one had been rejected, and two others were expecting to be called up. Mr. Mather remarked that the family had done very well if there were four brothers in the Army. The Tribunal decided that appellant should serve also.

div.head: WOMAN LABOUR TOO DEAR;
div.p: WOMAN LABOUR TOO DEAR;

Supporting the appeal of his son, who acted as farm manager, • farther said he could. not get .wconan labour. ' Women were getting 20s. to 245. per week in the works, and he could not Pay that figure. He had another son on the farm and he was "starred."
Air. W. Furness suggested that he should put himself to some inconvenience and let one Son go,
",I don't think so," replied the farmer. "I cannot get men. I am short now, and I am be- hind with the work."
One Month's exemption was granted on ,the understanding that an effort would be made to get someone else.
DECISION FINAL.

In another appeal for exemption of a farmer's son, where other two sons were employed, Mr. Furness said it was reasonable to ask that one on should go. Tribunals in other parts were doing this. _ _ _ .
It-\vtas explained in this case that one son's time was occupied in looking after his father, who had had a nervous breakdown.
The Tribunal refused exemption, and, on being informed of the decision, the man asked for the decision to be reconsidered. He said he did not know what to do owing to the short- age of labour.
-The Chairman intimated that the decision Was final.
WHY ONE AND NOT THE OTHER?

A firm of leather insniufactUrers appealed on behalf of a clerk and two workmen employed in one of the departments. The three men are married, and the Tribunal refused exeniption to the clerk and the youngest ,of the two WOrkmen.
The representative of the firm., on being in- formed of the deeision, asked, "Why it should be one, more than the others" The Chairman: We cannot go into particulars, sir._ That is. the decision.
The representative, as he left the room, re- marked, "I thank you, hut I think it is very unjust?'

A firm on Government work appealed,on behalf of two carters, one of whom was a foreman. It was stated that one of the men, about whom doubts were expressed as to his fitness for ser- vice, had gone before the military medical officer on Tuesday for examination, but the result of the examination had not been made known. The foreman carter was granted one month's exemp- tion, and the appeal of the other man was refused.

div.head: APPLETON RIFLE CLUB.
div.p: APPLETON RIFLE CLUB.
Opening Of Outdoor Shooting
Season.

The Appleton Rifle Club commenced the out- door shooting season at the Appleton Quarry Range on- Saturday afternoon, under first-class- 'weather conditions. Owing to the. absence on active service. of the President (Lieutenant. WALKING STICKS FOR WOUNDED SOLDIERS.
Mr. W. Stewart Royston Says £l,OOO Has Been Raised.
LETTERS FROM ALL Q 1 ‘RTERS.

Mr. W. Stewart Royston, of Sunnyside, Pad- dington, has this week sent us a few extracts from some of the letters he has received from various parts of, the world, from people who have heard of his effort to raise funds for the Purchase of walking sticks for wounded soldiers. About a month ago we published in, "The Examiner" an article from the Pen of Mr. Royston, under the heading of "A V.C. Worth Remembering," written after a visit paid him by Piper. Laidlaw while an inmate of the Lord Derby Hospital. That article has been read far and near, and Mr. Royston asks us to expos his grateful thanks to the Many Who have sent congratula tions and donations to the walking stick fund. There has," he says, "been such a stream of letters that it is quite impossible to say `.Thank you by 'Post to all, and I have not a private secretary, nor has the Postmaster-General given his permisgon as yet for free postage stamps to those Who perform acts of serbice for the benefit Of the State. But I do endeavour to send a pencil line to all who send a donation to :the Wounded Soldiers' Walking Stick Fund, as well as acknowledge each individually through the columns of 'Great Thoughts,' as all who read this inspiring weekly are Well aware.
FROM PHILADELPHIA AND SALT LAKE CITY.

"Letters continue to arrive from all parts of England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales, and from New York and—PhiladelPhia;. and last .week one came all the war ,from the Pacific Coast, whence a ..very .kind old gentleman ,not .only sent me a third donation, but .added "'I am going to write to the "British Cali- fornian," the "British . American," and the "Daughters of Empire," about your walking stick fund, and hope something may come to you for it.'" Miss Maud Dobson, who has sent a donation all the way from Salt Lake City, Utah,. U.S.A., .says it is difficult for •people in America to realise what the great war is from their own " poor-cold" newspaper reports, and she enjoys receiving newspapers from friends in England because one can rely on the news they contain.
• THE NEED STILL GREAT.

There are many withholfling their contribu- tions, especially in Warrington, because they -haVe heard of several hundred going to the Lord Derby War Hospital and other military hos- pitals in the town, and think there is no need- to contribute anything to the fund. If those who think so could inspect a few of the many appeals they would quickly. change their opinion. Only the other day the Matron of the Paddock House Hospital, Accrington, wrote "I can assure you that some walking sticks would be much appreciated by the brave men here, as so many of them are lame with 'trench feet." -

By the time this appears in print the "brave men" at Accrington will have ieceived a good supply. Having been informed fro n ancther quarter how welcome some walking sticks would be for the wounded soldiers, Mr. Royston sent fifty to the Woodlands Hospitals at Wigan dur- ing tlie present week! Lance-Corporal "11. Brazies, who has been in that splendid institution, the Roehampton House, writes:. "I must thank you very much for your kind gift of two walking sticks you sent , me; they are just the things I want before ielir ing London for .Bristol." A generous Scot, who frequently visits France on business, writes: "I am enclosing 10s. to- wards your stick fund, and hope it is getting on well." Continuing, he writes hopefully of . the. war, saying: "The German Chancellor's speech, prepared ,by the Emperor, was a tissue of lies, but they are only deceiving themselves, and histery will write them down in their own; colours: It is a nation •that • will never take a foremost 'place' in our world 'again; Meantime; we are going to beat them, and all their arm-

div.head: MAJOR CROSFIELD.
div.p: MAJOR CROSFIELD.
Septic Poisoning Still A Source
Of Darieer.

We regret to state that while the latest re- ports concerning the condition ,of Major (Temporary Lieutenant-Colonel) G. R. Crosfield do not give cause for any addifional anxiety, they do not; on the other hand, convey re- assuring tidings; such as we should have liked to receive after so long a time as has elapsed since the gallant officer was wounded. It is a case of serious septic poisoning and the best that can be said is that the medical and surgical authorities in charge of the hos- pital consider that Major Crosfield is doing "fairly well "---as well as they. coul4 expect "where so much septic poisoning has got into the system." . As is usual in this class of case, Major Cros- field's condition varies from day to day. The wound still has to be kept open, but notwith- standing this painful. and 'dangerous circum- stance,, his constant anxiety has reference to the earliest possible moment at which he may get back to his work with the battalion. In sending us the material from which we have been -able to extract the above authentic facts, Sir Arthur Crosfield. says :

"My eldest sister, Mrs. Ryan, has just returned from France, and she evidently felt before leaving my brother that he had gained some ground; my sister, Miss Crosfield, left early this morning to take her place, and we are all very thankful that one of " the family can be with my brother. That is naturally a comfort to him, and it saves him effort at a time when absolute rest and quiet is the Sort of medicine h. needs." •

div.head: MR. HAROLD SMITH, M.P., AND THE PERSIA.
div.p: MR. HAROLD SMITH, M.P., AND THE PERSIA.
What The Barber Wrote.

Mr. Harold Smith, on Tuesday in the House of Commons, asked the President of the Board of Trade: Whether on 12th March last the late hairdresser on hoard the Ss. Persia addressed a letter to the solicitor to the Board, alleging that no boats were ready to launch in case of. acci- dent.

Mr. Runciman : The witness referred to made a statement on February 7th ate a letter on March 12th. The letter was a pr.otest against the abandonment of the inquiry, and was not replied to. There was a large body of evidence to show that the boats were in good order and properly equipped, and that they were all swung out (except four carried an deck), and ready for lowering at the time the ship was struck. Mr. H. Smith asked whether the right hon. gentleman would not, in. view of the grave allegations contained in the letter of a some- what important officer, at any rate answer his letter.

Mr. R,unciman said that the letter was a pro- test against the abandonment of the inquiry, and did not contain allegations. Mr. H. Smith: The right hon. gentleman is entirely misinformed. I have seen a copy. Mr. Runciman : Even if those allegations were contained in the letter, I should not 'regard the hairdresser as an important witness. (Laugh- ter.) The Board of Trade must be guided by the main body of evidence, and that was quite clear on the point. Mr. H. Smith: Were not the statements of the hairdresser confirmed by passengers?
No reply was given. a Submarine Death Roll.

Replying to Mr. Harold Smith, Mr. Runci- man said the number who had lost their lives through enemy submarines or mines in the merchant service since August 4, 1914, was 3,117. of whom 1,754 were seamen, 188 fishermen, awl 1,175 passengers.

div.head: WARRINGTON FRIEND.
div.p: A WARRINGTON FRIEND.

A thoughtful friend who 'has been passing through a great sorrow, and With whom all Warrington has Sympathised, says:—" I do visit the Lord Derby Hospitaloccasionally, and always come home refreshed to, see the cheerful: spirit of the men. We had two soldiers to tea, ,and they were very anxious not to forget their sticks, so I told them how a .rrave invalid I knew had put forth his efforts; tO get them, arid they were pleased! A New Zealander who was here, said: 'it' is 'not what we 'get in people's homes, but it is the.feeling, of pleasure that it gives to be in a: home and.to h chat round. the fire that we like so Mad&

These words, says .Aft. 10Y5144, Alonld Cheer that friend of mine and theirs, " who4e'Motor car has been a Godsend to huadreds of wounded soldiers when at the Lord:Derby Hospital since the outbreak of war." "It will interest readers of' The Examiner, especially those who have sent two and. three donations, to know that when paying in.my last collection to the headquarters of the Wounded Soldiers' Walking Stick F.und,,r.T,was informed that the amount sent in had just, totted up one thousand pounds! Don't run. away with the idea that I have raised this big sum. I have simply done my litle bit! and mean to do a big bit until the war ends. We want another £l,OOO for walking sticks!

"The cOuntry wants. our sitter and the country needs, our service, wherever .the latter is freely given.. 'Don't turn. your back on it—go out to help them.' The days of petty jealousies are past, we are living in very serious times, and we shall need a 'pull' of every man, woman and child if we are to keen our Empire! It would be a nightmare to me .to• be a conscientious coward at home doing nothing for the 'brave who have suffered for us."'

div.head: CASUALS OF MILITARY AGE.
div.p: CASUALS OF MILITARY AGE.
Local Government Board's Instructions To Boards Of Guardians.

• Workhouse officials are to keep a keen eye on any casual paupers of military age who visit the Workhouse, and report their presence at once to the nearest recruiting officer. At a Meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guard- ians held on Tuesday afternoon the Clerk read a letter froom the Local Government Board si ing that Mr. Long had had his attention called to a few cases in which persons described as being single men of military age had received relief in casual wards. The Army Council had requested that all eases of men apparently of military age receiving relief should be notified to the nearest recruiting officer. Mr. Long wished to point out the advisability of det4in- ing cases of this kind for the full statutory period, unless action was taken by the recruit- ing officer before the expiration of that period. The Chairman (Mr. Linaker, jun.) said in- structions to this effect had been given to the officials of the Workhouse.

div.head: DONE!
div.p: DONE!

The matter was also before the Warrington 'Guardians On Wednesday, when the Clerk (Mr.. A. Bottoraley) said that what the Local Govern- nient'Board' desired had already been 'done in the Warrington rnion.

div.head: WARRINGTON APPEALS IN CHESHIRE.
div.p: WARRINGTON APPEALS IN CHESHIRE.
" My Conscience Will Finally
Decide."

A youth, nineteen years of age, who employed in a Warrington soap works, and lives in Cheshire, applied to the Cheshire County. Appeal Court at Chester on Tuesday for exemp- tion on the ground that he had a conscientious, objection to fighting or helping in the war. It. was, he said, impossible to serve two masters., He chose to stand or fall by the King of kings., whom he had undertaken to serve and who, to, him was, far more than an earthly king. He; must be faithful to Him, us he would have been expected to be faithful to King George if he had promised to serve him. He could not help to destroy life.which.Christ came two saves and he was Pkwepared to _take the .consequences' rather than violate his conscience.' .He refused. to attend wounded soldiers because when the, Germans fired a shell they intended to kill o man and not wound him, and if he (appli- cant) assisted in helping a: wounded soldier it would only be that the, soldier could go back: to the war, and the Germans .would then rectify their mistake and kill the man out- right. ,The Chairman said that was special pleading.: Asked by the Chairman what sacrifices he had made, appellant said he had a chance to go into munition works fel.- better pay, but he would not do so.

The Chairman said that was negative again. Had he given his goods to feed the poor, as the Bible enjoined? Appellant said his means would not allow him to do so. He did all he could to help anyone in need.
The Chairman: The appeal will he dismissed. Appellant: bly conscience will finally decide the matter.

div.head: WIDOW AND HER CHAUFFEUR SON.
div.p: THE WIDOW AND HER CHAUFFEUR SON.

There was a pathetic incident at the Che- shire County Tribunal on Tuesday when a' widow appeared before the Court clinging to the arm of her son, and seemed to be dis- tressed. She asked the Court not to take this son from her.

• Appellant, a young Warrington chauffeur, stated that his life was a hard one. He earned 30s. a week and gave 275. towards the upkeep of the home, which consisted of his widowed mother and deaf and dumb sister, aged 24, and two young relatives. There was no (Aber relative in the world who could Tender them assistance.
The mother of the applicant pathetically ap- pealed to the members of the tribunal to spare her ion.
"I want my son, do spare him, gentlemen, for me,' she said.
The Chairman said he thought that as the mother was so distressed it was undesirable that he should remain in court.
Applicant, however, asked for her to be allowed to stay. The Tribunal granted exemption until Sep- tember 1.
Applicant: Thank you very much, gentlemen. The mother: "Thank you, gentlemen!' This exemption iv'as the longest granted that day by the Tribunal.

div.head: WAR NEWS IN SALT LAKE CITY.
div.p: WAR NEWS IN SALT LAKE CITY.
"Stirring Arguments" Despite Neutrality Adjuration.

Mr. W. Stewart Royston, of Paddington, has receive&the following letter from a lady in Salt Lake City, Utah, U.S.A., who also enclosed a donation to his. fund for walking sticks for wounded soldiers:— " It seems hard for us out here, 7,000 miles away, to realise what the European War really means, for newspaper reports at best are but Ipoor, cold things. I enjoy getting the English newspapers which friends sometimes send me— or did before the CRnsor became 80 strict—be- eause• one can rely on the news ,the contain. Our American newspapers show a simply alarming talent for invention in the Matter of war items; in Salt Lake we have two rival morning and two evening sheets, and, each appears to vie with the other on the number of times they can kill the Crown Prince and the hundreds of people they can slay in Zeppelin , raids.

"This city is an extremely cosmopolitan place, I am sure almost every nationality must, be represented. .Personally I am acquaintel with, besides lots of British, French, Swiss, German, Italian, Greek, Japanese, Austrian,. Norwegian, Swedish, Cuban, Hawaiians and Maoris, not to meT4ion others which I don't know. There are lots of negroes and to say nothing of a Chinese' . colony in a, salubrious district known as Plum Alley—where ' the police are constantly making midnight raids on opium dens and gambling saloons! In such a city you will imagine what stirring times we have when a war argument is in progress, for although President Wilson adjures us all to be neutral, how can we be? There is always an excited crowd around each of our newspaper's office windows, discussing the latest war bulletins in,various degreels of. the English language. It's funny, really, and the corner policeman has to keep the tail of his eye upon them, to prevent the discussion becoming too violent!

div.head: TIIE OLY3IPIA, LIVERPOOL.
div.p: TIIE OLY3IPIA, LIVERPOOL.

The Olympia, Livali6ol, fiat week, will have an entirely cinema: bill, and it is the first occasion upon which an entertainmnt of this description has occupied the whole progralnms at any of the halls on the Moss' tour. "The • Birth of a Nation" will be screened by Mr. D. W. Griffith, whose master mind and soulful spirit -conceived the film. It is one of the biggest productions of the film world, and it contains 18,000 characters and 5,000 scenes. It took eight months to prepare, and the elaborate plant laid down for the perfection of photo- graphing the battle scenes by night alone cost £l,OOO. It is stated that £lOO,OOO was spent on the construction of the film. "The Birth of a Nation" takes three hours to screen, and, Mr. Griffith has leased the Olympia. for an indefinite period. There will be two performances daily, and Warrington people visiting Liverpool these holidays should not fail to see the film.
Thelwall Heys Hospital. The "special needs" .for Pound Day at the Thelwall Heys Military Convalescent Hospital, next 'Thursday,- will be handkerghiets, _note- , paper, green vegetables and -fruit.
