div.head: litct±trs to the (Oita
div.p: litct±trs to the (Oita
THE REV. 11. T. DIXON: THE CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTOR ?.

Sir,—lt has seldom, if ever, been my- lot to : meet with a more pitiful exhibition of cowardice ' than that portrayed in...the last two letters of ,• your clerical correspondent. ;A fortnight ago Mr. Dixon said that he was • prevented from defending himself by the pro- visions of the "Defence of the Realm Act." That statement is not true: Mr. Dixon is pre- vented solely from giving public expression to i what he calls his "conscientious convictions" 4, by the fear of possible consequences, and so, to save his skin, he keeps his mouth shut. I Mr. Dixon's, reference to the "Miner . : named Smith from Abertillery " furnishes the most complete . proof (it any fur- thor evidence. is needed) of the accu- racy with which I have defined his attitude. i' The rest of your reverend correspondent's letter is sheer impertinence and beneath notice He r ' 1 - rests content with " having drawn the badger PP ' -4 am more than satisfied with the opportunity , he has afforded me of exposing the " opinions " of a small, dangerous, and utterly selfish body ; of individuals, who claim every advantage which , . i 4 our citizenship affords and at the same time f repudiate all liability to such service as the , needs of the State, in this grave hour of peril.
1 deraand •
IT. ROBERTS.

div.head: MR. CHARLES DUKES.
div.p: MR. CHARLES DUKES.

1 3 Sir,—Permit me to congratulate you upon your impartiality in referring, in your last issue, to l'the recommendation that Mr. C. Dukes, and one or two others, who really represent a very small { section of the working people, and those not the most generously disposed, as representing labour, for inclusion on the Naval'and Military I, War Pensions Committee. I Although well aware that advertisement is the very breath of life to Mr. Dukes and many .; of his kidney, I must submit that the appoint meat of Mr. Dukes and those associated with him, would go beyond the bounds of ordinary decency. Is it right that a man who stated that at a meeting of the Trades Congress he took pleasur in hearing, and I presume in helping to sin; some 'song concerning a "Red Flag?' should be set to deal with those wounded men who 'have helped to keep the Union Jack, the real- flag of freedom, flying? The writer, all of whose sons have answered their country's call, wrolld not like any of them to appear before Mr. Dukes or anv of his sort, and would consider it a disgrace to receive the slightest help from them. KEEP THE OLD FLAG FLYING.

div.head: DRUNKENNESS AND RESMIC-
div.p: DRUNKENNESS AND RESMIC-
TIONS.

Sir,—ln reply to Mr. Parkes: The four weeks immediately preceding the introduction of their restrictions is the period .taken by the Control Board for purposes of comparison, is I stated. Mr. Parkes' comparison of five months in 1914 with five months in 1915 is not really of muea value, as in the latter period the male popula- tion had been greatly reduced by enlistment. Mr. ,Parkes 'entirely pooh-poohs the possibility of any manipulation of drunkenness arrests; perhaps he will explain the Government's guilty silence when Sir John Rees brought this charge forward in the House of Commons. _ _

Your correspondent concludes with the fol- lowing patriotic proration: "These restrictions are only part of the larger question 'Drink 'or victory?' The Tsar of Ithssia answered Victory France answered ' Victory '; and what shad we answer?" Mr. Philip Snowden, perhaps the most active and fanatical teetotaller on the Control Board, answers " Stallmate." England cannot win, says this gentleman; an"' yet people like Mr. Parkes would bolster up these wretched restrictions as essential to tho triumph of the Allies!
3. E. SIMPSON.

div.head: FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.
div.p: FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.
HOUGHTON GREEN ODDFELLOWS.

At the annual meeting of the " Sir Gilbert Greenall " Lodge (Loyal Order of Oddfellows). held at the Plough Inn, Houghton Green. on Saturday, Bro. George Mather, of Fearfthead, was elected President for the ensuing year. lie has held the position of President of. the society for 48 successive years. The balance presented was regarded as satisfactory. The President said he felt proud to be at the head of a society which had made It faithful .promise to keep its soldier members straight on the books so that when they returned to civil life they would receive the same privileges and benefits as be- fore. On the motion of Bro. Samuel Wilker. seconded by Bro. George Higham, a hearty vote of thanks was passed to Bro. Mather for pre- siding.
At the meeting of the Tribunal a member passed a remark about the clock being stopped. The military representative replied that it was a war-time economy. Economise in time e'er it is too late.
A short time ago a comedian at the Warring- ton Hippodrome passed a gag to the effect that Lymm was not quiet, but unconscious. He evidently has not been in the right place at the right time.
Which of the Warrington theatres is the most popular. to Lymm patrons? Both are well patronised.
I think that the 9.45 train from Warrington is run chiefly for the benefit of Lymm play- goers. It is always full up at Latchford and empty at Heatley.
Favoured by good weather ,and plenty of sun- shine, Lymni should be a popular ,resort thi Easter.
The universal question this week is: "Rave you got your Blue Cross ticket yet?"
A High Legh Will—The late Mr. Samuel Massey Houghton, of Swineyard Hall, High Legh, farmer, has left £8,049.
Easter Furloughs.—lt is expected that a large number of "Derby men" will be home for Easter. Two have already arrived, namely, Privates J. Ravenscroft and F. Read, both of the Cheshire Regiment.
On The Bench.—There were on the Bench at the Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Messrs. A. Welkin (chairman), A. W. Callender, J. T. Ridgway, H. Holden and the Hon. J. E. Cross.

The Lighting Regulations.—At the Sessions on Wednesday, James Moston, Booth's Hill, and Robert Dandy, Brookfield-terrace, were sum- moned for failing to comply with the lighting restrictions. The case against Moston was adjourned; and Dandy was fined ss. Cycling Offences: Trouble With His Lamp.— Bernard Hardy Moore was summoned at the Petty Sessions on Wednesday for riding a motor cycle without a year light after dark.—Defend- ant stated that he had had a lot of trouble with the lamp as the door was loose, and the wind blew it open and blew the light out.— Fined ss. , _ _

Harold Saunders, Booth is Hill, was fined 2s. 6d. for riding a cycle on the footpath at Warburton.—P.C. Bolsover proved the case. Punishment Increased.—At the Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday, William Ackerley, labourer, Partington, was summoned for in- decent-conduct.—P.C. Bolsover stated that when asked for his name and address, defendant gave a false one.—Defendant said he thought it was "a strange policeman."—The Chairman re- marked that they intended to _fine him 55., but awing to the fact that he had given a wrong tame they decided to fine him Ds. John Lowndes, Partington, was 'fined ss. for indecent conduct.—P.C. Bolsover proved the case.

Must Pull Himself Together.—Thomas Leigh. Statham, was sumomne,d at Lymm on Wednes- day. for using obscene language in Bridgewater- street—Defendant stated that he had been in ill-health for some time, and was upset owing to the fact that he had had a son killed in thn war, and another wounded.—P.C. Davies proved the case.—ln fining him 2s. 6d., the Chairman stated that there were twelve previous convic- tions against defendant, but owing to the fact that he had lost a son at the war they had dealt leniently with him. Defendant must pull hiniself together in the future. Rush Green Man Provoked To Wrath.— Walter Wright, Rush Green, was summoned at the Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday for using obscene language in his house on the 18th of last month.—Defendant pleaded guilty under extreme provocation.--P.C. G. R. Davies state-I that he was passing defendant's house when heard someone using very bad language. De- fendant came out, and when asked about the language, lig replida"There is no one speaking." —Defendant, giving evidence, stated that he had had a long spell of work, and when he came homer there was no light in the house, lie knocked his head against the mantelpiece and lost his temper.--Five previous convictiOns proved against him, and he was fined 7s. 6d.

div.head: 11, FOR WOUNDED SOLDIERS.
div.p: 11, FOR WOUNDED SOLDIERS.

Probable Utilisation Of A Portion Of Dutton Workhouse. The probable utilisation. of a portion of' the Dutton Workhouse for wounded 'soldiers was referred to at a meeting of the Runeorn Board of Guardians, held on Tuesday afternoon. The matter was, mentioned by the Chairman, Mr. C. E. Linaker, jun., who said the Medical. Officer had been in communication with Colonel Goggin, the military medical officer for the area. respecting the housing of 20 to 25 wounded soldiers in spare rooms at the Workhouse. The maximum amount of 3s. per man per day had been offered, which was the same as paid to voluntary hospitals. The question of the cost of, putting the rooms into proper order, decorating. and furnishing, had to be considered, and an estimate had now been prepailed. The ordinary builder's work was estimated at £lO5, and he (the Chairman) assured the Guardians that the money would not be thrown away. It would be capital value for the fixture. • The decoration of the rooms might cost £3O. The total expendi- ture under this heading would be £135, and it was a maximum amount. It. was•estitnated that £l5O would be required for the purpose of pro- viding beds, fully, equipped, and that was con- sidered a most reasonable cost. The total outlay for the accommodation of 20 to 25 wounded soldiers was £285. There was also the -question of the nurses' room, and the matron had agreed to ,sacrifice her 'drawing room, and this would •lend itself to the whole scheme. The Emergency Committee had passed a reso- lution recommending that the offer of wounded, soldiers be entertained on the conditions laid down by the military authorities. , The Chairman further pointed out that the present bedding in the institution was out of date, and at the end of the war the bedding used by the wounded would be useful. A Member: Will it 'be worn out? The Chairman: It will all depend how long the war lasts. , We may all be worn Out. (Laughter.) A Member: What about the cost of nursing? The Chairman: We shall want tWO nurses. A Member: Who will Pay for them? The Chairman said they would pay for the nurses out of the allowance made by the mili- tary authorities. Mr. Linalcer, sen., was in agreement with the proposal to provide accommodation for wounded soldiers. He -did not see how they could refuse: as public men to support the recommendation of the committee. He, however, could. foresee difficulties if the beds were not always fully oecupied. Mr. Lister Kaye also agreed on the same lines, and said if the beds were not always occupied the 3e. per day per man would hardly be suffi- cient for their maintenance. The Chairman pointed out that the question before the Board was the amount they intended to spend on the equipment of the place. Mr. Piling thought it peculiar that the mili- tary authorities, having accommodation else- where, had come to them. The Chairman thought that as their medical officer had brought the matter forWaid, he might be able to strike the right note with Colonel Geoggin• It was agreed, on the proposition of Mr. Lin- ulcer, Ben.. .that the military authorities should be asked to inspect the accommodation, and-that it should be explained what the Guardians could do. and alsh that a further report should be madtvoirtheimbJect.

div.head: MILITARY TRIBUNAL. Bank Employe's Case Heard In Private.
div.p: MILITARY TRIBUNAL. Bank Employe's Case Heard In Private.

_ A bank employe applied for a, further -exemption for dOmestio reasons, having pre- viously been granted temporary exemption until April 14th. The case was heard in private and finally adjourned. Farmer's Claim for Son's Exemption.

A farmer applied for a further exemption for one of his sons, this son having previously 'been granted temporary exemption until the 14th. He stated that this son was employed as a dairyman and cowman on the farm, which consisted of 40 acres cultivated land, 43 acres grass, 36 cows and 6 horses. The son worked an extensive milk business. He had two more sons working on the farm, one single and one married, and a boy. At a previous sitting of the Tribunal the claims of the remaining two sons *ere ‘heard, but they •failed to put in an appearance and their claims were disallowed. The Clerk remarked that these two sons had lodged an appeal to be heard before the Appeal Tribunal zit Stockport. It was further state& that the son whoge appeal was now being heard was the only one who had voluntarily attested. ' The case was finally adjourned for a fort- night,' the Chairs:can remarking that in the meantime they inlaid possibly know how the other two sons had fared before the• Appeal Tribunal.

div.head: Gave Up a " Starred " Occupation.
div.p: Gave Up a " Starred " Occupation.

A cycle agent and repairer applied for total exemption, stating that Ue was the only cycle repairer in Lymm and that he repaired all the Past Office cycles. It was, he claimed, in the interests of the public that these cycles should be kept in good condition, as they covered a very scattered area. He did a lot of work in the cycle line for munition workers. He fur- ther Stated that he was a skilled mechanic, and on the outbreak of war he left his occu- pation purposely to relieve a man in the Poet Office who had been called to the colours as a reservist. Had -he remained where he was he would have been in a "starred" occupa- tion. Ho further stated that in doing this he had made a sacrifice, as he could have tkarn:hi better wages if he had kept to his trade. The Chairman (Mr. T. J. Ridgway): Could not the Post Office cycle work be done by a man over military age? Applicant: Yes, it could be done if the man was capable of doing The Chairman: How much time do you. spend on the Post Office cycle work? Applicant: About one ftdi. _day a_week, sir.

It further stated that applicant was a married man with three children (all young) and that he had been in the cycle business about five years. The Tribunal decided to grant temporary exemption until the 30th of May. Why the Milk Dealer Attested.

A milk dealer applietl for total exemption on business and . domestic grounds. He stated that he sold 330 gallons of milk weekly and supplied 250 families. It was isio the national interest that this work should be carried on. If he was called to the colours he would lose half lis.lbusiness.
In answer to the Court lie said 'his wife

div.head: Ex-Volunteer, Fire Brigade Superintendent And Prominent Freemason.
div.p: Ex-Volunteer, Fire Brigade Superin- tendent And Prominent Freemason.

Lymm has this week had cause to mourn the loss of one of its most popular residents, Wm. Kirkpatrick, of the Bridgewater Arms. He was the head of a fine patriotic family, the whole of his three sons being with the Colours. Two have been on active service about eighteen months; the youngest has not yet attained his nineteenth birthday. Mr. Kirkpatrick him- self was an Old member of the 3rd Volunteer Battalion Cheshire Regiment, and was forced to retire under the age limit several years ago. with the rank of Pioneer-Sergeant. For this

div.head: LATE SERGT. W. KIRKPATRICK.
div.p: THE LATE SERGT. W. KIRKPATRICK.

service he was the proud possessor of the Volun- teer long service medal. About 40 years ago he became connected with the local fire brigade, under Superintendent Harrington, as a fireman. His ability was speedily recognised, and he became the brigade superintendent, and held this position up to a few 'months ago, when he was forced to retire by' ill-health. On his retirement he was highly complimented for his work by the Urban Dis- trict Coimcil.

div.head: Funeral.
div.p: The Funeral.

The funeral took plaee at the Parish Church on Monday afternoon, when a large number of inhabitants assembled to pay respect to his memory. The cortege proceeded from his residence, through the village, up the Church green, thence to the Church. The coffin was carried into church by four local gentlemen, Messrs. Win.:Moston; F. Guest, T. Knowles and E. Edwards, when a short service was held by the Rector (Rev. G. B. Thurston). The bearers from the Church to the graveside were four members of the local fire brigade, Superin- tendent 'Wm. Rose (deceased's successor), Engineer Simpson, and Firemen Hinton and Downwood. There were also present at the graveside several deputations, namely "Chester P Lodge of Freemasons.—Bros. F. Dean, W.M. ; A. M. Higham, P.M. • F. Jefferson, S.D.; W. G. Groves, W.P.M.P., G.S„ P.R.; W. Daniels, H. Holt, P.M., and Westwood.
The Old 3rd Volunteer Battalion, Cheshire Regi.raent.—Ex-Colour-Sergeant W. G. Groves. Urban District Councit—Councillor W. G. Groves.

Wreaths and lioral tributes were sent by "Beloved wife and family," "Chester" Lodge of FreemasOns, Fire Brigade, "Ernest and Harriet; also Little Joan," "Jennie and Wil- liam," "Brother Hugh' and Wife," Grand- children, G. White, "Andrew and Edith," "Nellie and Harry," "Mary and John," "Brothers and Sisters—jess, Charles, Dorothy, Maggie and Jeanie."
The funeral arrangements were conducted by Mr. W. G. Groves, of Booth's Hill.

div.head: SAPPER PERCY CLARE.
div.p: SAPPER PERCY CLARE.
HI In Hospital.

8-113 Per Percy Clare, of the Royal Engineers, whose home address is Booth's Itill, has been admitted into hospital suffering ,from a general breakdown. Writing to his mother at Booth's Hill, the gallant soldier says—" I am on the improve. As you will see, lam still in hos- pital, but don't worry; there is nothing the matter with me worth worrying about. I have just got run down a little, but will soon be all right again. I think I have been- very lucky, for since I Ave been out here I have had noth- ing the matter with me worth mentioning. Since I have been with the Engineers I hav3 been in the tienolles 'eYery day; and if not in the day, every night, so I have a lot to be thankful for. I have had some very narrow escapes, but I think it is as you say, that GA is answering our prayers, and there is nothing like prayer. It is just fourteen months to-day since we landed here, but I don't think we shall be apart for another fourteen months, if only I have the luckto pull through. Just keep on smiling and look on the bright side of things, and think about the time you will have 'when the boys come home.'" At the commencement of war Sapper P. Clare was a Territorial, but soon after getting on active service he was transferred to the Royal Enzineers. Tn civil life he is employed as a gardener at West"Legh, and is a prominent foot- ball, being connected with the local club.

div.head: PRIVATE GEORGE TAYLOR.
div.p: PRIVATE GEORGE TAYLOR.
'Wound That Almost Proved Fatal."

Private George Taylor, Rush Green, has this week been discharged by the military authori- ties in consequence of being medically unfit for further war service. He was employed as a major's groom, and was jumping into a trench on July sth, when he fell on a bayonet, which passed through his body near the lower rib, and came out in his side. He was conveyed to a Canadian base hospital, and there lay between life and death for four months, before he was fit to be removed. He was eventually sent over to a hospital in London. He says: "Words 'cannot describe the kind treatment I received while in hospital, for I received everything I wanted, and everything that was possible to be done for me was done, and .done cheerfully, for • although there were thousands of other soldiers undergoing treatment they were always ready to inconvenience themselves for our comfort." Private George Taylor waS mobilised at the outbreak of war, and was eventually drafted out to the Front early in February of last year. In civil life he follows the occupation of a teamsman in the employ of Mr. Samuel Davies, -Platt Farm, Heatley. With a look of disap- pointment he remarked that he would have to give up working in that sphere of life and look out for a lighter job. He was educated at *Dughtrington Scbool,and worshipped at Ought. rington Pariah Church.

At the Lymm Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Collin Stevenson, lodging-house keeper, of Partington, was summoned for having allowed Louis Hiebeck, an American subject and an alien enemy, to reside in his house without having registered the fact to the police; and Louis Hiebeck was charged with being an alien enemy and failing to register.—P.C. Bolsover stated that on the 2ard of last month he called at Stevenson's house and found that he had an American living with him. When asked why he had not registered the fact with the police, he pleaded ignorance of the law. Witness "showed him the papers outside the station and told him he would be reported.— Stevenson said that had he known he had to register he would have done so. He had a son at the War.--:-Hiebeck, giving evidence, stated that being an American he thought it would he all right. .Had he known he ought to register he would have done so willingly. The Chairman, 'in 'fining :them. each 10s.„ re- 'mhrked that the 'Bench Were willing to believe their Story, but it was a case in which a .penalty had 'to be imposed.

Wife of a German. • Mary Ellinor Rohmer,. of :§andY:lane. Was stinimoned for being,an alien:Spetn.Y and 'failing to register.—Sergeant Davies -Atated that, along :with P.C. Atherttin, ,he called 1:41 defendant on the 28th ,of lust -montlito make inquiries. When .ofeltdant opened the door she remarked, The long-exPeeted has arrived:" They, were in plain clothes at the time.—lloerner, giving evidence, denied Milling this statement, and said that when She answered the door she was not alvtite that they were Police officers. She had to SSlc them who they were and then 'asked them inside. Asked What she did say, she replied: "If I had to, -register, 'how long a time you have been in 6oming." Asked by,•the•ChairMan hOw long her huSband 'had been dead, She replied several years.—ln. fining .her .305., the Chairman said they were Sorry to convict,, as she was an English woman; but by Marrying a German she had taken hi's nationality.

div.head: UNREGISTERED ALIEN ENEMIES.
div.p: UNREGISTERED ALIEN ENEMIES.
Lodging-house Keepers Must Be Very
Careful.
INCREASE OF WAGES 'OR BONUS?
Dispute At The Salt AVolfks Ends In
Police Court.
WORKMEN PAY DAMAGES.

An interesting case came before the magis- trates at the Lymm Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, when Messrs. Charles Moore and Co., Ltd., Lynam Salt Works, claimed damages from two workmen, John Adamson and Samuel Wright, for leaving work without notice. There were cross-summonses, by Adamson for the recovery 'of 11s., which was the amount of pay for two days' work, and also for the recovery of damages, caused by the withholding of his insurance card; and by Wright, for the re- covery of 9s. 10d. (two days' wages) and also damages caused by the retention of his insur- ance card. A third workman, Edward Hewitt, claimed from the firth the amount of two and a half days' pay. Rise Refused; Bonus Granted.

Mr. Greaves Lord, barrister (for Messrs. Moore and Co., Ltd.), said that the different plants in the works worked_ in co-operation, and if one failed all failed. The men knew that the work was extremely particular. Re- cently the men became satisfied that they wanted an advance in their wages, and on the 10th March a number of them, including Adamson, Wright and Hewitt, gave a week's notice, saying that the 'reason they did so was that they wanted arise in wages of sixpence a shift. The manager of the works proposed to see the men. at five o'clock on ,the 10th Mtlrch, and he told them definitely that the firm would not give them the advance of sixpence a shift, but that they were'perfectly, prepared to make another suggestion 'which' would work out in the long run at a larger amount They were prepared to give a bonus. It ,was talked about, and a minor alteration was suggsted. by the men, and Dr. Trantom withdrew their notices, and from that time they turned up for their work. The bonus arrangement, was a very valuable arrangement, because it gave the workmen something to work for, and ensured the masters a good carat) for any advance thtfy' might make. The men worked•bn, and as show- ing that the bonus was a good one, the result of the first week's work was that Adamson became entitled to an advance of 55., and the other men something between 3s. and 4s. The arrangement was made so - that the bonus should be paid monthly.

div.head: Defendants Dissatisfied.
div.p: Defendants Dissatisfied.

Apparently Adamson and 'Wright were not going to be satisfied, and on Friday, the 17th inst., they ceased work. They got their wages in the ordinary Way, but they did not ask for their insurance card, and, what was more, they accepted their week's wages, which were paid on a Friday. They thus hud two days' wages. owing when the men came', iii to work on 'the five o'clock shift. Adamson and •Wright tried to get them not to start work. Hewitt was one of the men who turned up to work on the five o'clock shift on Friday evening, and was marked as starting work at five o'clock. Adam- son and Wright went to the men and persuaded some of them to leave the work—among whom was Hewitt. The result was that volunteers had to be got together, and there was a de- crease in the production of work to the extent of ten tons, and much damage was done tO the plant—much more than the firm had sum- moned for. When Adamson and Wright should have come back they did not do so. Mr. Lord said they had only summoned the two men, who they thought were the ringleaders. If the conclusion was come to that the men had improperiy terminated their employment, the firm had no desire that anything should be done in the matter beyond the awarding of nominal damages. They did not want anything like the present charge to happen in the future.

div.head: Evidence.
div.p: The Evidence.

Dr. William Trantom, managing director of the firm, spoke to refusing the men the six- penny rise on the shift, but offering a bonus, which was to be paid monthly, as near as pos- sible. Adamson knew perfectly well that if the plant upon which he worked was stopped, then tbe others would also be stopped. In answer to Mr: Rhodes, Dr. Trantum said he was not aware Wright had applied for work at the Partington Steel Works, but had not been taken on because he did not possess an insurance card.
dalnes Thomason, emploxed, in the pay' office at' the Salt Works, said that' the men did not ask for their insurance cards.

John Nixon, timekeeper and storekeeper, said Hewitt came to work at five o'clock. and some time afterwards sent away with Adamson and Wright. John Adamson said he Rave his notice to the foreman on the Friday, Vie 10th inst., and also went to draw his money. Ha admitted that if the salt plant was stopped the others would be interfered with. •Not A Legal Notice.

The Bench retired for about a quarter of an hour, and upon their return the Chairman (Mr. A. Watkin) said the I3ench unanimously found that the employment was not terminated by legal notice, and there would be damages for breach of contract against Adamson and Wright. which they put at £1 each, including costs. These were nominal damages as desired by Dr. Trantorn. In regard try the two flays' par owing to Adamson and Wright, and two and it half days' to Hewitt, the snmmonses would be withdrawn on the undertaking of the company to pay the money.

Mr. A. Bottomley proposed the re-election of the retiring overseers, Messrs. Jas. Whitley, F. Warburton and F. Peamon.. This was tarried, and it was decided to place on record an appreciation of their services. The overseers re- turned thanks, Mr. F. It was decided, on the proposition of Mr. Bottomley, to place on record an apprecia- tion of the services of Mr. E. Bradshaw, assistant overseer.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.
PARISH COUNCIL.
Compliments Plentiful At The Annual
Meeting.
The annual meeting of the Stockton Heath Parish Council, held in the Church Institute on Tuesday evening, lasted only half an hour.
Chairman Re-elected.

Mr. H. J. Westbrook, in. proposing the re- election of Mr. W. -Mclntyre as chairman, said he had been a very useful chairman. He hoperl that peace would be declared this year, and then they would be able to say "Rise, Sir William." (Laughter, and applause.)—Mr. J. Hallows seconded, and the motion was unani- mously carried, Mr. Mclntyre thanking his fellow members for their renewed expression of confidence in him.
Overseen.and Assistant Overseer.

div.head: Accounts.
div.p: The Accounts.

Mr. Bradshaw presented the Parish Council accounts, which showed that the year wa, started with a balance in hand or £4 18s. 7cl. while the balance now in hand was £4 12s. Bd. The care of trees had cost £6 10s.

The accounts of the overseers for the half-year ended 30th September, 1915, were also presented. The overseers commenced their work with a balance in hand on the poor rate of £665 10s. 7d., and finished with a balance in hand of £636 Is. 10d. On the special expenses account there was a balance in hand of £47 4s. 9d.

Mr. Bradshaw, in answer to a question by Mr. Bottomley, said that some of the rents of houses had gone up, the assessments being correct. There was less cottage property empty, but rather more larger property. The calls for the half-year had been about the same.

On the proposition of Mr. Bottomley, the statements were adopted. There were present at the meeting :—Messrs. W. Mclntyre (in the chair), P. Pearson, J. Hallows, C. W. Hallows, H. 3. Westbrook, F. Rose, J. McDermid, A. Bottomley, F. Warbur- ton and E. Bradshaw (clerk).

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Rummage Sale.—A rummage sale organised by the sisterhood in connection with the Wesleyan Church was held in the schoolroom on Friday evening last week. A large assortment of articles had been collected from various sources, and when the sale opened at seven,o'clock there was a large number of ready buyers. Great in- terest was centred in the museum, where a large number of curios, kindly lent by members of the congregation and friends, had been very tastefully arranged by Mrs. Dakin. One could not help but wonder how such a magnificent collection had been got together. Some of the years specimens exhibited were over 400 old. There were drapery, refreshment, and pound stalls. Hot suppers were a great attraction. At intervals duets were sung by Miss J. Ward and Miss J. Dewar. The proceeds, which were in aid of the trust funds, realised Xl7 Bs., which, after deducting expenses, leaves a net profit of SAG 10s. for the trust.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

Unneighbeurly Neighbours.—At the Warring- ton County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before Mr. Roger C. Parr (in the chair). Mrs, Blink- horn, 5, Lock Cottages, Penketh, was fined 204. and an advocate's fee for assar!lting Hannah Thompson and Dora Harper, residing at 1 and 3, Lock Cottages. Mr. Swallow, solicitor, who appeared for the complainants, who were mother and daughter, said that the parties resided in the same row of cottages. On Tuesday, march 7th, Mrs. Thompson was returning home 'after making some purchases in the Tillage, when the

defendant approached and used abusive and threatening language. Defendant followed Mrs Thompson , into her house, and words led to blows, and complainant was struck several violent blows in the face and also was bitten on the hand. Her daughter, Dora Harper, was also struck in the face.—Defendant, who pleaded guilty to assaulting Mrs. Thompson, said there was provocation for the assault. The conduct of her neighbours had made her life miserable.

div.head: HILL CLIFFE.
div.p: HILL CLIFFE.

Baptist Church.—The Sunday school anniver- sary services were held on Sunday,„ the preacher being Councillor R. morning and evening Henshall, who spoke in the morning from IL Kings vii. 2, "Behold, if the Lord would make windows in heaven, might this thing be," and In the evening from Psalm lxxxiv. 6, Who passing through the valley of Baca make it a -well." Anthems were given by the choir at each service, " Sun of my soul" and "Behold, how good and joyful." Mrs. Ken.worthy and Miss Capell took the solos. Little Lottie Morris (a scholar) delighted the congregation by her sweet solo, " All things bright and beautiful," which was given in perfect style,. and made a deep im- pression. Solos were rendered by Miss May Isherwood, "Nearer, my God, to Thee," and "0 Divine Redeemer "; the ease and beauty of Miss Isherwood's voice make her a great favourite. Mr. J. Turton, too, sang in fine style "A dream of Paradise" •and "Thanksgiving." Mrs. Roughsedge was the organist and Mrs. Ken- worthy choir leader. The accompanists were Mrs. Massey, Mr. Cyril Pemberton, Master Booth, and Mr. A. Fairclough. A children's service was held in the afternoon, when the chairman was Mr. H. Brocklehurst, and the address on "The Mariner's Telegraph" was given by Mr. J. S. Richards, an address which was full of thought and highly beneficial to the young people. Not the least part of these ser- vices was the sweet singing of the scholars under the leadership of Mr. George Moss. The pieces were "Stand for the right," "Golden hours," "The commandment of love" and "My Saviour's Voice." Notwithstanding the inch, ment weather, there were good congregations all day, and this happy and prosperous anniver- sary was brought to a close with the national hymn, "God bless our native land." div.head: COST OF LIVING.
div.p: COST OF LIVING.
Increased Charges For Outdoor
Relief.
RUNCORN GUARDIANS "STUBBORN,"

A difference of opinion between the Warring- ton and Runcorn Board of Guardians respecting the payment of increased out-relief to a woman for whom the Runcorn Board accepted liability, was referred to at a meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, held on Wednesday, and it was decided to lay the facts before the Local Government Board and ask them to advise the Runcorn Guardians thereon._ _ _ _

The case was mentioned by the Clerk, who said the woman had been resident in War- rington for many years, and she had always borne a good character and had had a comfort- able home. ' She and her husband agreed to separate many years ago, and he made her an Allowance up to some few years ago, when owing to age, he was unable to continuo it. The woman managed .for ,two years without troub- ling the Guardians,7bUtler Son then got married and shen Niles etiMPelled to apply for relief. The Guardians granted her out-relief, but as the case belonged to the Runcorn Guardians the Warrington Board asked for a settlement. The Runcorn Board acknowledged liability, but refused to give relief outside their own Work- house, which meant the woman would have to break up her home. The Warrington Guardians, at their own instance, granted out- door relief, and instructed the Clerk to do everything in his power to induce the Runcorn Board to pay. For a time the son returned to live with his mother, and during that period no payment of relief was made. Shortly afterwards a fresh application was made to the Runcorn Guardians to grant relief, and they did so, and it had continued up to the present. Recently, owing to the increased cost of food, kc., the Warrington Board decided to increase the amount of relief, and asked the Runcorn Board to approve bf the 'action. This they refused to do. _ _
Several Guardians expressed the view that the Runcorn Guardians had acted very stubbornly in the matter.
The Chairman (Mr. A. J. Jolley) said although it, was only a question of moral pressure, they were fully entitled to use every influence they could to secure decent treatment for a deserving case.
On the motion of Mr. J. W. Knowles, seconded by Mr. W. J. Shaw, it was agreed to take the action as stated above.
EXTRA ALLOWANCE FOR ROMAN CATHOLIC CHILDREN.

div.head: FOOD PRICES.
div.p: FOOD PRICES.

The Clerk stated that the Army Service Corps had sent 'a list of prices, the idea being to con- sider the advisability of substituting contract Army supplies for local supplies at the White- cross Military Hospital. According to the table of prices, the Clerk said he found that the Hos- pital Committee were purchasing sugar at 9s. per cwt. cheaper, tea id. per lb. cheaper, and flour is. 9d. per 1401 b. cheaper than the pricea given by the Army Service Corps. No action was taken.

div.head: REDUCED "CALL."
div.p: REDUCED "CALL."

4 The Clerk reported the receipt of the county precept, which. amounted to .213,704 12s. 5d., a decrease as compared with the corresponding period of last year of £560 and of £4B on the pre- ceding half-year. DIARIES AS USUAL.
A 'brief discussion took place on the question whether the Board should issue new diaries or just have a leaflet issued for the current twelve months.
Mr. Knowles proposed the printing of slips. and Mr. Shaw moved as an amendment that new diaries and backs should be obtained.
Mr. Shaw's amendment was carried by nine- votes to eight. THE MENTAL WARDS.

A report was read from the inspector of the Board of Control respecting a recent visit to the mental wards at the Workhouse, which stated that the inmates appeared to be happy, and made no complaint, except on the score of de- tention. Cards, dominoes, draughts and other games were provided for them.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

There was little business of public interest at Tuesday's meeting of the Runcorn District• Cou- ncil, held at Dutton Workhouse. Mr. T. Antwis was reappointed chairman, and Mr. W. Harri- son vice-chairman. MAINTENANCE OF LIVE STOCK.

A circular letter was read from the Board of Agriculture and Fisheries, stating that the ex- emption provided by Act 2 of the Maintenance of Live Stock Act, for calves bred from cows of prescribed dairy breed had been deleted owing to the fact that the exemption had led to an evasion of the Order. The price limit of 30s. prescribed had been raised to 405., and pro- vision had also been made for the slaughter of calves in districts where markets are closed owing to the foot and mouth disease restrictions.

div.head: WORKMAN WHO WAS LATE.
div.p: WORKMAN WHO WAS LATE.

Mr. C. E. Linaker, jun., wanted to know what supervision there was over the Council's work- men, and he cited the case of an employe who had been seen going to work at 8 o'clock in the morning, when he should have been there earlier.

Another member complained of the laxity of the Council's officials, and it was agreed on the proposition of Mr. Linaker, sen., that the Assistant Surveyor should be provided with a diary, and that the same should be presented to the Council at each meeting for examination.

div.head: FAILED TO REPORT.
div.p: FAILED TO REPORT.
Ex-Territorials Not Within Scope Of The Compulsion Act.
HOWARD DISCHARGED,

Thomas Howard, a well-known -Socialist, :3, Preasziok.street, who was arrested it the .hills of Sootland last week on a charge of failing to report himself under the Military Service Act, was again brought before the Borough Court en Monday, and on the application of the Chief Constable was discharged from custody. The Chief Constable explained that /Award was before the Court on Thursday last,when an :adjournment was agreed upon till Wednes- day. A solicitor, who represented defendant, said ,helad a good defence, but did nettidisclose it then. The prosecution had since learned that kdefendant had served four yews -in the local Territorials—from 1908 to 1912—end as the provisions of the Military Service Act did not amily to men who had accepted service in the Territorials, he asked that the case should be dismissed and Howard discharged- Phis course the military authorities had agreed to. Accused said he had nothing to say.

_ •_ •The Chief Constable said when accused ap- Tedled.to the Tribunal he said gime tthe:age of eighteen he had been.,against war. After that 4ige he served four years in the Territorials. Accused did nOt know that he W S therefore excused from military service._ _
Accused was accordingly disebarged. MR. BRANDWOOD'S POSITION.

We understand that Mr. Harold Brandwood; who was before the Court las week along with Mr. Howard, has proved that he, too, has serve .1 in the Territorials, and so obtained his uncon- ditional discharge.

div.head: WAS WAITING FOR THE OFFICER.
div.p: WAS WAITING FOR THE OFFICER.

Thomas Taylor, a conscientions. cobjector, 2, Percival-street, was at thel'Boiongh Court on •Saturday ()barged with failing to report him- self for military service. • Detective Green gave evidence to interview- ing accused at his residence on Friday. He ;naked him why he had not reported himself, and accused replied that he had been waiting for the officer to come. He further -stated that he had received a certificate for non-combatant 'service from the County Tribunal, and he understood that the local Tribunalho.d not been notified. _ _ _- -

The Chief Constable said accused should have reported himself, and the matter colikl have been dealt with by the military authorities. Accused appealed to the Tribunal on ‘conscien- Cons grounds. A fine of 40s. was imposed. The Chief Constable asked for an alternative to be imposed, so that the police could ,deal with accused if he was certified as medically* lasifirt. The magistrates decided that the alter- native should be 14 days' imprisonment.

div.head: FURTHER REMAND.
div.p: FURTHER REMAND.
Could Have Enlisted" If Ile Had Wanted.

An Irishman named Wm. Corcoran (82), who Was remanded a week ago on a charge of failing to rePort himself under the Military Service Act, was further remanded for a week at the Police Court on Wednesday, in order that the police might complete their inquiries. The Chief Constable said the police were under the impression that the prisoner had been staying long enough in England to make him arnenable to the Service Bill. Directly an in 7 timation was received from the Home Office 'the prisoner would be brought before the magis- trates. When arrested by Detective Green he replied "I could have joined in my own country if I wanted." He also admitted having been in England since Christmas.

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
HOUSEWIFE DUPED.
Smart Sentence On Liverpool Men
With Bad Records.

The borough magistrates on Tuesday sen- tenced Richard Turner, 9, Back Aston-street, Liverpool, and Thomas Shnfflebottom, 23, -Upper Dalton-street, to three months' imprisonment each, on a charge of obtaining £1 Is. by false pretences from Ellen Flannaghan, of 34, Gee- street. _ _

The Chief Constable said that on Tuesday morning last the accused offered a piece of oil- cloth for sale, stating that it had been left over after they had done some work at an hotel in the vicinity of the Central Station. They told Mrs. Flannaghan that they were not hawkers, and wanted her to have a bargain, as they did not wish to sell it to brokers. Believing accused's statement that the oilcloth would cover two rooms, she paid 21s. After they had left it was found that the oilcloth was not suffi- cient to cover one room, let alone two. Detective-Sergeant Reddington said he had made inquiries at hotels in the vicinity of the Central Station, but could not find any trace of the prisoners having laid any oilcloth or linoleum. _ _ .

Mr. G. Wilding, furniture dealer, said a fair price for the oilcloth was 'l2s. Mr. -Steel, who represented accused, sub- mitted that it was not a case of' false pretences. Although accused would not give evidence they denied that they made the statements as alleged by the prosecution. 1e submitted that Shufilebottom had nothing whatever to do with the transaction; he was simply in the employ of Turner.

The Chief Constable said Turner was brought to the Police Station some four years ago on a coMplaint of attempting to perpetrate a similar offence, and he was then caution.ed. Turner started his criminal career in 1908, and had a long list of previous convictions against him. Shufflebottom, added the Chief Constable, had an equally bad record, having started his career in 1903.
On the application of th 9 Chief Constable, the magistrates made an order for 21s. to be re- funded out of the money found in Turner's possession.

div.head: REFRAINED FROM ENLISTING
div.p: REFRAINED FROM ENLISTING

Because lie Had Sores On His Head. Percy Fox, no fixed abode, who appeared at the Warrington Police Court,on, Tuesday charged with failing to report under the Military Service Act, wat remanded until Saturday to enable the policylß make inquiries. _ .

- Ile Chief Const.alible said that the accused was arrested at the Union Workhouse on Monday morning. He (accused) said he was quite will- ing to enlist, but had refrained from doing Si because he had sores upon his head, and be thought he would not be accepted for military service.

The Chief Constable asked that the case should be adjourned so that accused could be handed over to the military authorities, who would decide whether he was fit for the Army. Prisoner was accordingly remanded.

div.head: HELPED HIMSELF
div.p: HELPED HIMSELF
And Shared Meat Pies And C.hoegazdes
Among Friends.

William Killgarriff, wire cleaner, and Joseph Barton, wiredrawer, were charged at the War- rington Police Court on Tuesday with stealing three meat pies and chocolates valued nine- pence, the property of Jack Clare, 60, Win:wick- street. Barton was alto, charged with receiving the property, , It appeared that late Son ,Moliday sight the two prisoners were in the prosecutors .shop, when Killgarriff was seen to take the pies an.l give one to Barton. Another pie was offered to a man who-was also in the shop. Killgarriiff also helped himself to chocolates. The prisoners were taken into custody by Inspector Stuart, and in reply to the charge _
Killgarriff said I. took them. I will ti11r.43 -the blame for it all." Ilarton said " I knew they were gtolen. and I threw them away."
The Chief Constable said there weve seven previous convictions against Barton.
Fined 20s. each.

div.head: TOO MUCH LIGHT.
div.p: TOO MUCH LIGHT.

A fine of 10s. was imposed upon Mrs_ lamp- oon, manageress of the British Workman Tea and Cocoa Rooms, Horsemarket-street, at t.13.*3 Boinugh Courtnn Tuesday, for contravening the Lighting Restriction Order on the 10th inst. P.C. Cameron said that brilliant rays of light came from the window of the shop and reflected on the street and the adjoining property. When he spoke to defendant she replied lam sorry; I did not Mink it Was so."

Defendant denied the accuracy of the officer's statement. She said the blinds were drawn and the lights were shaded. She, had done her utmost to shade the lights. Richard Stephens, 8, Watkin-streot, was also fined .10s. for a similar offence. •

div.head: SAN KEY STREET DANGERS. Batch Of Manchester Motor
div.p: SAN KEY STREET DANGERS. Batch Of Manchester Motor
Lorry Drivers Fined.

The borough magistrates on Thursday were engaged for two hours in hearing cases against a number of motor drivers in the employ oi the Cotton Industry Transport Co., of Manches- ter, for driving motor lorries at a speed danger- ous to the public in the narrow part of Sankey- street and Liverpool-road, on the 28th ult. Mr. Heaton, Manchester, who represented the firm, asked that the hearing of the cases should be adjourned to a future date; in order that the manager of the firm could attend Court. He complained that the solicitors had had no time to prepare an adequate defence, and the circum- stances were so varied that they had no data upon which to work. The motor drivers were continually on the road, and the company had not been able to interview them respecting the summonses. At the time of the alleged offences the men wore never stopped, or warned, and some days elapsed before they were summoned. The Chief Constable opposed the adjournment, and said ample time had been allowed fbr the preparation of the men's defence. He read a letter from the firm stating that they would not allow their drivers to act contrary to the restrictions, and if they had received notice of the offences they felt sure their drivers would have acted strictly in carrying out the require- ments, and the offences for which they were sum- moned would not have occurred. Special arrangements had been made that day so that the cases could he heard. The Court decided that the summonses should be proceeded with, and evidence in support of the offences committed by defendants in Sankey- street and Liverpool-road were given by Sergeant Hayes, P.C.'s Cameron and Harrison, and Special. Constable Dendy.
-High Speeds For Narrow Streets.
The lorries were driven at estimated speeds of 14, 16 and 18 miles per hoer, the latter rate

being estimated in Li'verpool-ro.ae. ifa;fng: re- gard to the narrowness of the streets, the con- gested state of traffic, and the number of side streets, the witnesses asserted that the speed wa, dangeious to public safety. The Chief Constable mentioned that in several cases tile defendants had been reported by the constables for dangerous driving at a different time on the same day as the alleged offence, and inb"lainces on the following day'. '' - _

When seVeral of the cases had been decided. Mr. Heaton suggested to the Bench that the other summonses might be dismissed on pay- ment of costs. He characterised it as hard that all these men should be brought to Court, when the fining of one or two would have acted as a warning. __

div.head: Numrous Complaints:
div.p: Numrous Complaints:

The Chief Constable said the Watch Com- mittee had considered the matter. Complaints had been so numerous and the police had been so castigated that they had been bound to take' action. Sankey-street tradespeople had com- plained and wanted to know why nothing was done to put down dangerous driving. The Chairman thought the fines imposed were very low. and defendants were being dealt with as leniently as possible under the circumstances. Defendants declared that they did not drive the lorries at more than three or four Miles an hour though the narrow part of Sankey-street. - Fines ranging from 20s. to 60s. were imposed.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 22, 1916.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 22, 1916.
NURSE eIIILD9s DERTFI.
Warrington Fester-Mother Sent For Trial On Manslaughter
Charge.

div.head: CASE AGAINST MALE DEFENDANT WITHDRAWN.
div.p: CASE AGAINST MALE DEFENDANT WITHDRAWN.

The borough magistrates on Monday dis- charged from custody Charles Goodwin, labourer, 2e, Cockhedge-lane, who, with his ,wife, Ellen Goodwin, of the same address, had been remanded on a charge of neglecting a two- year-old boy, now dead, of whom,Mre. Goodwin was the foster-mother.
Coroner Brighouse last week held an inquest on the body of the boy, the accused being in attendance. The jury returned a verdict of "Manslaughter" against Mrs. -Goodwin.
when she got it. and called it 'Ethel Goodwin. The child was still alive, and was four years of age on the 4th or sth February last.

div.head: HUSBAND DISCHARGED.
div.p: HUSBAND DISCHARGED.

At the Borough Court on Monday, Mr. Browne, who appeared on behitif of the Direc. Or of Public Prosecution,, referred to the charge of neglect preferred against Charles Goodwin, and said he had had a joint consul- tation with the Chief Constable and Inspector Wainwright, of the N.S.P.C.C., with respect to what should be done with the male defend- ant, the Director of Public Prosecutions having practically left the matter in his hands. Seeing that the Coroner's jury did not commit him to the Assizes, and seeing that he had been in custody fourteen days, and with other circumstances connected with the case, which they had thoroughly discussed, he had come to the conclusion that the better course would be to ask that the case be adjourned. The Clerk: You offer no evidence? Mr. Browne: That is so. _ . _
—.--- Mr. Steel, who represented accused, said he had often thought whether there was a case against accused, and he asked that he should be discharged. Accused was discharged from custody.

div.head: MRS. GOODWIN CHARGED.
div.p: MRS. GOODWIN CHARGED.

Ellen Goodwin, who looked very haggard and depressed, was, then charged with "Man- slaughter," .and Mr. Browne, in outlining the case for C prosecution, said the deceased boy, who formed the basis of the charge, was for- merly known as Charles Goodwin, but his proper naI:AA was found to be Henry Edge. If the Court found that a/Atria-facie case had been made out againseprisoner, he asked that she should be committed to the Assizes. In consequenr of a serious report received by the Inspector of the N.S.P.C.C. a visit was paid to accused% home at 10, Naylor-street, which was found to be in a filthy state. The child, now the subject of the charge, showed signs of real neglect, with the result that Dr. Peacocke was called in, who examined the child and ordered its removal to the Union Infirmary. The child was seen there by Dr. Binns, who would speak of its gross neglect. Accused obtained the boy from Nurse Pierce, 20, Laurel-road, Fairfield, Liverpool, who kept an accouchement establishment, and who had had several transactions with accused. Nurse Pierce brought the boy to Warrington, handed him over to accused, who also received Xle and signed an agreement. The child was insured for a certain amount.

div.head: BABY-FARMING ALLEGED.
div.p: BABY-FARMING ALLEGED.

ge •alleged that, taking all the suspicious circumstanCes and the way accused went about, it was really a case of baby farming. Only last month accused received a baby from London, for which she received £2O. One could not but come to the conclusion that where a woman received sums of money---. 420 and £10— it was to her advantage that such children should be got rid of. Accused had children of, her own, and there was no need of other children. She had never notified the Clerk to the Board of Guardians that she had nurse. children. • •

Evidence was then called, and Dr. Peacock° repeated' the evidence given before .the Coroner's jury, which was to the effect that when he was called in to see the child on March 23rd it was suffering from bronchitis and had all the appearances of being neglected. The house was in a filthy condition. The child must have been ill several days before he was called in. - _ -

In reply to Mr. Steel, witness said when he visited 10, Naylor-street, he was given to understand that accused intended to remove to Cockhedge-lane. Accused told him she had been using home remedies to counteract the child's illness. - Dr. Binns, who conducted a post-mortem examination, described the child's body as generally emaciated. It only weighed 14i1b., whereas the.. average weight of a child of two years was 321 b. He formed the opinion that the child had been suffering a long time and had been neglected. He attributed death to bronchial pneumonia, accelerated by starva- tion.
In reply to Mr. Steel, the doctor said in the post-mortem examination he found no trace of tuberculosis. He agreed that teething chil- dren sometimes rejected their food.

div.head: CHILD INSURED.
div.p: CHILD INSURED.

An insurance agent in the employ of the Blackburn Philanthropic Assurance Company, Ltd., said he was approached by the accused to insure the deceased. Accused gave the child's birth as taking place on February 9th, 1914. The company issued a policy on the life of the child for a penny per week, under which policy, accused would be entitled to ..£'6 at death.
Answering Mr. Steel, - witness said the de- ceased had been in full benefit since March, 1915.
Mr. Browne: Shortly, before the death of the child were there considerable- arrears? '

Mr. Steel protested and the question was ruled out. Nurse Kate Maria Pierce, .20, Laurel-road, Fairfield, Liverpoefi, •tr- -certified, midwife told the Court that the deceased child, which had. been registered as Charles Goodwin, was really Henry Edge, the illegitimate child of Mary Edge. The child was born at her house on 9th February, 1914. She did not register the child and did not know where the mother was now. Witness knew accused as "Mrs. Spencer," and had corresponded with her in that name.- Pre- vious to witness handing over the deceased to accused, witness had had previous transactions with her. She brought tho baby to Warring- ton and met accused either at Bank Quay Station or the General .Post Office. She had destroyed all the letters received from Accused and signed "Mrs. Spencer," with the exception of one (produced).

div.head: BABY "NOT STRONG."
div.p: BABY "NOT STRONG."

in reply to Mr. Steel, witness described ,the mother ,a the deceased as "not. strong." The baby was prematurely born and was very small. She told accused that deceased was not strong and would require a lot of care. By Mr. j. Sefton, Liverpool (who watched the proceedings on behalf of Nurse Pierce): It was not her duty to register the child. Detective-Sergeant Reddington gave evidence to executing the warrant for the arrest of accused. He visited 10,-Naylor-street, but found that accused had left. He arrested prisoner at Cockhedge-lane,- and in reply to the charge pf, neglecting the child, she said: '!I have nothing to say, only I have not been cruel to it Whenl .prisoner had been in custody two days . she expressed a desire to make, it.,statement to tell. the truth about everything'. She'said : "About 'four years ago she sttw an, advertisement in a Liverpool paper stating that a Nurse Pierce, took in women pending accouchement and she wrote to her, .asking if she had anyone who wished to place out .a child, as she would adopt it and bring it up' as 'one of her own. She 'received a reply to the effect that she had a child then at her house, whose, mother had died, the father having - deserted them, and that she would give her £1 per month for five months or £5 down to take the child, which money she would pay out of her own pocket. She agreed to take the child and the ES and went over to Liverpool, where she was met by Nurse Pierce' at the Central Station. She signed an agreement and brought the child back to Warrington with her. She did not register the. birth of the; .child, nor did she receive a birth %certificate when she had the child given to her. It was three months old

div.head: VISITS TO LIVERPOOL.
div.p: VISITS TO LIVERPOOL.

"About two years last May Nurse Pierce wrote and told her that a lady wished some- one to take her baby and asked her to go to Liverpool. She went to Liverpool on a certain date and was handed a boy by the nurse, which was then three weeks old. She also received piece of paper bearing the.. child's name, but she could not say whethei:it'was a birth certi- ficate or not. The child was called Frank, but she could not, ,remember its surname. She also received ,Xl.O, but she could not remember giving a receipt for this. She took the child back .to Warrington with her, and at the age of three months it died from meningitis, .Dr. Manson,.iyho..had attended:"it,. giving_ a certi- ficate to that effect. She returned the paper to Nurse Pierre, and informed her that the child was dead. She registered the death as that of Frank Goodwin, the child of herself and her husband."

div.head: HANDED OVER WITH £lO.
div.p: HANDED OVER WITH £lO.

In February, 1914, she again wrote to Nurse Pierce, asking if she had another boy she could have, and she received a reply stating that she had a boy, and would bring it to Warrington. She met Nurse Pierce at the General Post Office. Warrington, where she handed her the child and £lO, for which she gave- a receipt in the name of Ellen Spencer, that being the' name by which she was known to Nurse Pierce. She took the child home, but did not register it. She called it Charles Goodwin. In November, Nurse Pierce wrote her a letter asking her if she knew of anyone who would adopt a baby girl, and she replied that she was willing to take it herself. She met her at Bank Quay Station, and received the child and £9 for which .she gave no receipt. She did not register the child, but called it Doris Goodwin. It was a fortnight old when she got it, and it died on 216th November, 1915, when seven weeks old. The. child was not seen by a doctor before death, but Dr. Liston was called in after death and he expressed his opinion that the , child might have died from convulsions, brought on by a sliglat attack of bronchitis_ The deaths; reported to the Coroner, but there was no in- quest.

- About six or seven months ago she saw an advertisement in a paper inserted by Mrs. Morris, the Avenue, 33, Bedford Park, London, which -stated she took ladies in for confinement. She wrote her, but received no reply, but on January tat, 1916, she received a letter from 'Mary Munday or Williams, who gave Mrs Morris's address, and informing her she was to be confined in February. She asked her if sill Would take her baby as its father had been killed in the war, and offered her £2O. She wrote and told her she would take the child. On March 16th, 1916, she received from her a postal order to diver her fare to London., She went, to -London the following day, and Mrs. Morris handed her the child at Euston Station, together with the birth certificate, and Z.-- for which she signed a receipt. She was told the child would-be a month old on 27th March, 1916.5 he never saw the mother of the child. She brought the child to Warrington. She did not register it, but called it Ronald Goodwin.

div.head: NEVER TOLD HER HUSBAND.
div.p: NEVER TOLD HER HUSBAND.

The statement continued "I have had four children of my own, three of which -are still alive, and one was stillborn. I never told' my husband that I Was going to adopt the children, but when I brought them homel tpld him where I had got the4l... froni, and what money I received for them. He was very arigry With me. He said he would do the best he could for the chil- dren. I always gave him a sovereign or so, and bought him some clothing, &c., out of the rest of the money. . I did not insure the lives of either Frank or, Doris, but on September, 12th, I insured the lives of Ethel and Charles, eac:i for a penny per week with the Blackburn Philanthropic Afisurance Co., Ltd., Carlton House Chambers, Sankey-street, Warrington. I in- sured them as Ethel and Charles Goodwin. The collector did not ask me any questions and I did. not tell him the children were not my own." When witness charged accused with " Man- slaughter'," she replied, "Well, sir, I did not kill him."
At this point the hearing was adjourned till Wednesday.

div.head: RESUMED HEARING.
div.p: THE RESUMED HEARING.

At the Police Court on Wednesday, before Mr. S. Wright, the hearing was resumed. Mr. A. Browne stated that he had been in communica- tion with the Director of Public Prosecutions with regard to.the ruling of Mr. G. White (the magistrates' clerk), who stated at the first hear- ing that evidence regarding any other children placed in the custody of the accused could not be accepted. He had received instructions to proceed with two other witnesses, and gave notice that further evidence would be given at the trial at the Assizes.

Nurse Hall, at the Warrington Union Hospi- tal, said the deceased was admitted to the hos- pital on March 23, suffering from bronchial pneumonia. Its condition was very bad, and gradually grew worse, and it died on March 27.

Inspector Wainwright, of the N.S.P.C.C., said that in consequence of receiving an anonymous letter, he, in company With Mr. John- Constable, intpector under the Infants' Protection Act. visited 10, Naylor-street, where the accused re- sided. He asked her if she had taken in a child to nurse, and she replied that she had. She also told him' that she had three children of her own—Lily (12), Ethel (4), and Charles (2). The latter was the subject of the inquiry. Thc!' house was scantily furnished an, Mt- tronely diftiebridilion. The back bedroom was in a filthy state, the floor being littered with rubbish, which accused stated was due to their pending removal. Mrs. Goodwin admitted that she received 275. to 28s. per week from her hus- band. On Thursday March 23rd, he again visited the house, and found her nursing the child. It looked thin, very ill, and, from the breathing, was suffering from bronchitis. Mrs. Goodwin said the child was suffering from the effects of teething. On his advice she promised to call in Dr. Liston. Obtaining the date of birth of the Child from the accused, he searched for the registration.of . his birth, but failed to find any entry. Later in the day he again called at the house, and ascertaining that a doctor had not seen the child, which was in a seriofis condi- tion, he conveyed it to the Workhouse Hospital. He asked for particulars about the child, and Mrs. Goodwin replied that the boy was regis- tered at 20, Laurel-road, Fairfield, Liverpool, and she got £lO. On March 25 witness obtained a warrant for the arrest of prisoner on a charge of neglect.

div.head: PRISONER'S STATEMENT.
div.p: PRISONER'S STATEMENT.
A statement made by the oritoner was read as followi •

div.head: COUNTRY TOOLMAKERS.
div.p: COUNTRY TOOLMAKERS.
Classified As "Ordinary Work- men" Under Munitions Act.

A large namber of tool makers workini; this district will be greatay interested in a decision which was 'givPn. by Mr. A. J. AEhtnii, K.C., at a general Munitions Court, held at Warrington on Saturday morning, when Messrs. George Plumpton, Ltd., were fined £lO for un- lawfully employing a workman of Mr. John Berry, of Ditton, he not having been given a leaving certificate. -The point of contention, submitted by Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor for the defendants, was as to whether the man John Brimelow, jun., of Crouton, was a Workman or not. His case was that not being employed on the premises of Mr. Berry, he was not a workman.

_ Mr. W. S. Knowles, solicitor, of Widnes, for the complainant,' said that for eight years or more, Mr. Brimelow, who lived at Cronton, had worked for his client in the making of tools, 'and Messrs. George Plumpton, Ltd., had taken I him away from Mr. Berry and given him employ ment before six weeks had elapsed. This was 'contrary to the Munitions Act. A ktterhad been written to Messrs. George Plumpton complain- ing of this, and stating that they had done it in face of the fact that they were "fully aware that the tool makers are employed on urgent Government work. Your methods have a tendency to make workmen dissatisfied. understand that /our latest visit was on Mon- day, and it is my intention to furnish the Admiralty with particulars of your indue?,- ments." In reply to that, Messrs. George Plumpton, Ltd„ had said:—" We have yet to learn that these country tool makers are any more yours than ours. We always thought that when the workmen worked on their own premises, using their own tools, they were ours as well as anyone elses." Mr. Knowles added that for thirty-three weeks prior to January 15th, when he ceased to rn:,ke toots for Mr. Berry, Brimelow was paid on an average £2 4s. 2d. a week. The man had been given regular employment, and Mr. Berry paid the ,employer's part of the insurance money regu- i larly. Like many other tool makers, he did not go to the factory every day, but, by arrange- ments with another man, worked in a worksho9 near his own home. Mr. Knowles, however, pointed out that he did things with Mr. Berry'; tools, and worked there purely for his own con- venience.

John Brimelow, jun., said that he had aske I for light work, but had not recently been able to get it with Mr. Berry, and therefore, owing to his ill-health, he had had to seek work else- where. He citified that Mr. Plurapton • had approached him. It was he (witness) wh3 approached Mr. PlumptOn. Mr. Browne pointed out that• there were a-great number of tool makers in this district, and if had been the custom for them not to give a weela notice. T:bey 'wore simply 'contractors, and not workmen. On Saturday morning some of them came to town from their own work- shops, brought their tools, and said they were gang to do no more. .That was the custom of the trade: They were not workmen in,the ordinary sense at all. In announcing the. decision of the Court given above, Mr. Ashton said he and his two assessors were clearly of opinion that those tool makers who worked on piece work, whether at home or whether in the factory of their employer, were workmen within the meaning of the Munitions Act The fact that they were paid piece work and worked at home did not make any difference. In fact they were work- men, and at his courts in the future 100, wouhl hold that.

div.head: MONDAY'S COURT.
div.p: MONDAY'S COURT.
EX-SOLDIER AND HEAVY WORK.

An ex-soldier, aged 29, appeared before the Munitions Court on Monday to support his application for a leaving certificate on Oh? ground that the work he was engaged upon was too heavy for him, and that he had been given a chance of a lighter job•in Liverpool. He was engaged as a wireweaver. Applicant had been in the Army up to October, when he was discharged owing to a wound: He hai only been employed seven or eight weeks. For the firm it was stated by Mr. G. M. Webb that applicant's description of the heavy work he had to do was a little exaggerated. Applicant • was employed on Work for men in the trenches. The firm was behind with its Government con- tracts, and every man the firm lost during the next four to six weeks would mean a serious reduction in the output. When applicant came to work he told witness that he would •" stand loyally by him'."

Mr. Webb described the application as a typical excuse of a man who wanted to leave for a lighter job. Applicant told him he had ft-illy recovered from the wound received -on servile. The firm was prepared to release applicant in four weeks' time. The case was adjourned till May *frt to enable applicant to produce a doctor's certinate.

div.head: DOING USEFUL WORK.
div.p: DOING USEFUL WORK.

A young man at the Warrington Munitions Tribunal on Monday gave his reason for apply- ing for a certificate of discharge that he wanted to join the Navy as an artificer, which he con- sidered was more usefui than the work he was now doing. The Court held that he was doing useful work, and refused a cert;ficate.

div.head: RIVETER AND HIS FOREMAN.
div.p: A RIVETER AND HIS FOREMAN.

A riveter applied for a leaving cer- tificate at the Warrington Munitions Court on Monday, on the ground that he "had been treated with no respect" by tho foreman, who, he alleged, told him he "would suffer if he did not work overtime."

In reply to the firm's representative, applimnt said his weekly earnings were £4 lOs. He Admitteti losing eight quarters and one day in six weeks.—The Court refused to• grant applicant a certificate. "

div.head: "REQUIRED LODGINGS."
div.p: "REQUIRED LODGINGS."

Young , Woman Said She Had ' Had Motor Breakdown. A young woman, a stranger to. Warrington, who gave her name as Alice Evans, was charged at the Borough Police Court 64 Wed- nesday with obtaining food and lodgings, by false pretences, and further with an offence under the Registration Act.

The Chief -Constable, in applying for a re- mand for a week, said that on Monday night the prisoner called at the house of Rachael Coyne, 44, Parker-street, and represented that she was employed by the GoVerement in the Motor Transport Section. In consequence of a breakdown with the motor she was obliged to stay in' the town, and' she required lodgings. Mrs. Coyne allowed her to -remain at the house, hut the next morning, becoming suspicious, she discovered that prisoner was walking about the park, apparently with nothing to do. ;The police were informed, and prisoner was arrested. From inquiries, it was ascertained that she had stayed at another honse. On each occasion she had given a false name on the registration form. A remand of seven days was granted.

div.head: PUNISII US :vlos7.
div.p: PUNISII US :vlos7.

Addressing th 9. annual meeting of 01.9 Lanca- shire Federation of Liberal Clha, (mks turday It. afternoon in the Castleton LiSA•a,ro 4':Roch- dale, Mr: A. 11. Illingworth,":lk ".,' n. 9 09d clivisiOn), said a question of sil. ' 5 4kil ' ' nee rg to this country had arisen Xec'es .1..._ 'el:ques- tion of "Tariff Reform, or =Proteltteil.: '' Some people thought it was more of a business pro- position than political. He himself considered a system of Protection was no business propo- sition. (Hear, hear.) He maintained that energy, efficiency, knowledge, and specialisation in trade were likely to be of more use in Cap- turing neutral markets than a tariff on imports of German goods into this country. We must have cheap raw material. (Hoar, hear.) It was the very life of the country. .. . i Let no one think he was not in favour of punishing Germany., 'Be had more., reason probably for wishing to punish Germany than any other man in that room; he wished to punish the Germans severely, but by going into ' a general system of Protection we were raore likely to punish ourselves than the Germans. i (Hear, hear)" He had ideas of punishment far more drastic than a general tariff, but. this was not the time to go into them. We had first to , beat the Germans—(bear, hear)—to destroy Ger- man militarism entirely. Wheti4.:we had done that it would be time enough to go into these 'questions. 1 Of course he did not say there were not some rindustries Which needed special consideration, especially -dyeing. ' Before the war the Germans 'hada monopoly Of- dyesimffs, which they works-1 against us in a military way which no one in this country at the time suspected. We must never be dependent again on Germany for dye- stuffs, and though it might .be necessary in this matter ta depart from our most cherished- tradi- tions it would be in the long run for the good of the country. But if we succeeded in destroy- ing the German military power as thoroughly s.s he hoped and believed we should there wouli have to be an indemnity paid. And how was that to be paid except in the form of 'Germau goods? Germany had no foreign investments to hand over to us. We could not take her rail- ways, and she could not pay us in gold. We must therefore take payment in goods; and tilt longer Germany was in paying us in that yiae the better it would be for us. because she would be kept • back,. from rebuilding her niilitary power.

England had been built up on Free Trade, and must not put that system aside while drunk with rage and dumb with horror at the atroc.- ties committed by a homicidal maniac; we must wait until we were more sober in mind an I able to look at the question with better judg- ment. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: Sir Ryland Adkins And National Unity.
div.p: Sir Ryland Adkins And National Unity.

Sir Ryland Adkins, M.P., for the Middleton division, in a letter which was read by the President of the Federation (Mr. C. A. Doran) wrote: "The greatest of wars is now at the turn for good or evil. Friends and enemies alike watch with intense interest what happens in England. Anything which awoke controversy here, especially anything which broke the con- tinuity of the Government, would give joy to Germany and weaken the confidence of the Allies. Mr. Asquith and Sir Edward Grey stand in, the face of Europe as the expression of our nation's indomitable will and. unshaken. fidelity. To support them and their colleagues indepen- dently of our views on this or that method. cf policy at home is the duty of us .all. I• do not anticipate any cleavage of Britisb„ opinion on the war or on international affairs, but there are always risks where harebrained or unscru- pulous critics have the means in Parliament ().- in the Press of misleading public opinion.!'

div.head: Hippodrome.
div.p: Hippodrome.
Miss May ‘Sherrard, who has scored a big sue- cess at the Hippodrome .this week, is a Lanca- shire woman, born in Liverpool, and she is a comedienne with a- style of her own. -

In a short chat I had with her in.her dressing- room she told .me that she was hooked up for the next five years on all the principal circuits, which speaks eloquently for her popularity with variety audiences. She is a pleasing little lady off the stage as she is on.. •

. She features comedy of. the broad type, and infuses any amount of life into her business. A. hearty laughter is better than doctor's medi- cine, and Miss .Sherrard with her songs makes every ,one feel happy and aroused.
The programme is packed full of good turns. Mr. Norman Payne is an entertainer who does not require a piano, but depends upon a host of good stories and a good voice to win him popular favour.

One of the most amusing turns of its kind on the vaudeville stage is the Keystone Comedy Cyclists, and Hippodrome audiences have greatly enjoyed their whimsical wheeling performances. They are aptly described as the "Barnum and Bailey of cycle acts."

"That remarkable war film. "Britain Pre- pared," has been a big attraction at the Hippo- drome matinees throughout the week, and has been much "talked. about." It is undoubtedly a cinema masterpiece. On Monday afternoon the audience included tire Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Peacock), Colonel Mogg- ridge, Captain Stott, Captain Mathams, anl other well-known townspeople. •

Hippodrome patrons are certain to have their, appetites satisfied during the Easter holidays, for I observe in next week's bill of fare, The Waldrons, " Joe and Etty," who top the bill. They are a live coUple, with an abundance of laughter-making comedy, and they are bound to "make good." The Three Sisters Mabarte are another tip-top turn. Charlie Bell and Company will present ".The Demon Photographer:" • It is said to be a side-splitter. The 'other Artistes supporting are Doris Broughton, Dorothy Arnold, The. -Monzo Trio, and Two Musical Hastings.
The Kinemas. Star K i nema.
A different • " star" picture each day, and every one so good as to satisfy the most exact- ing critic, has been the rule at this popular Picture house during the week.
Perhaps the best of the bunch was "Rags," featuring Mary Pickford, shown on Wednesday night to a crowded 'house. •
For; the holiday week a fine programme has been arranged. Easter Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday the "star" film is entitled. The Bad Lad ,of the Family." :
"The Bad Lad" cannot be so very dreadful, as we are told that the film is one long laugh from start to finish and full of rollicking fun, just the rigbt sort of • tonic for war-time. • •
"The Explorer," . adapted . from W. S. 3faughan's book, will he screened on the three latter days of next week„
Mr. Tellegen, formerly leading ,man with Sarah Bernhardt, takes the principal part in "The Explorer." •
Patrons are advised to watch for the coming of "The Pop Doctor," an adaptation of the famous novel that was read by over 3;000,000 people.
"The Pop Doctor" is an all-Eritish produc- tion, featuring Miss Agnes, Glynne and Fred Paul.
